title: IP, Addressing & Routing

lessons.title: Read the IPv4 header
lessons.summary: Read the fields that describe an IPv4 datagram and interpret its header-length and total-length limits.
lessons.body:
The **Internet Protocol** (IP) has one job: get a packet from one host to another, across any number of networks, on a best-effort basis. It does not promise delivery, ordering or protection against duplicates. Those are left to the layers above (TCP) or to the application.

That modesty is the point. Because IP asks so little of the networks underneath, it runs over Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 4G, fibre and satellite links alike. Basic forwarding examines the IP header and a forwarding table; real routers also apply validation, queueing and policy.

The unit IP moves is a **datagram** (often just called a packet). Each one carries its own source and destination address and is routed independently. Two packets from the same download can take different paths.

## The IPv4 header

Every IPv4 datagram starts with a header of at least 20 bytes. Here it is, 32 bits per row:

```
0       8       16      24      31
+---+---+-------+---------------+
|Ver|IHL|DSCP|EC|  Total Length |
+---+---+-------+---+-----------+
| Identification    |Flg|FragOff|
+-------+-------+---+-----------+
|  TTL  | Proto |   Checksum    |
+-------+-------+---------------+
|        Source address         |
+-------------------------------+
|      Destination address      |
+-------------------------------+
|   Options (0 to 40 bytes)     |
+-------------------------------+
```

Field by field:

| Field | Bits | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Version | 4 | Always 4 |
| IHL | 4 | Header length in 32-bit words |
| DSCP / ECN | 6 / 2 | QoS traffic class, congestion marks |
| Total Length | 16 | Header + data, in bytes |
| Identification | 16 | Groups fragments |
| Flags | 3 | Reserved, DF, MF |
| Fragment Offset | 13 | Position, in 8-byte units |
| TTL | 8 | Hop budget |
| Protocol | 8 | What's inside |
| Header Checksum | 16 | Accidental header-error check |
| Source / Dest | 32 each | Addresses |

A few details worth knowing:

- **IHL** (Internet Header Length) counts 4-byte words, not bytes. Options add header bytes and can encounter filtering or slower processing, depending on the option and equipment.
- The **Total Length field** is 16 bits wide, so it caps the size of a whole datagram. Basic Ethernet commonly carries 1,500-byte IP packets, but other links, jumbo configurations and encapsulations have different MTUs.
- **Protocol** tells the receiver which handler gets the payload: 1 is ICMP, 6 is TCP, 17 is UDP.
- **DSCP** (Differentiated Services Code Point) marks traffic classes, for example "expedited forwarding" for voice. **ECN**, when supported by endpoints and the network, permits congestion marking of eligible packets; it does not eliminate all packet drops.
- The **checksum** covers the header only, not the data. Because every router decrements TTL, a forwarding router must update it, possibly incrementally. IPv6 has no corresponding header checksum.

Two length fields use different units, and mixing them up is a classic parsing bug:

- **IHL** counts 4-byte words. The usual value, 5, means a 20-byte header; the largest, 15, means 60 bytes, of which 40 are options. The transport header (TCP, UDP, ICMP) starts straight after however many bytes IHL says, so software that assumes a fixed 20 bytes misreads any packet carrying options.
- The **Total Length field** counts bytes and includes the header. Being 16 bits wide, its largest value is 65,535 bytes. In practice the link MTU, usually far smaller, is what limits real packets.

## Key takeaways
- IPv4 provides best-effort datagrams; each packet carries its own addresses.
- IHL counts four-byte words; Total Length includes header and data.
- The header checksum excludes the payload and must change when TTL changes.

## Further reading
- [RFC 791: Internet Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc791)
- [RFC 1812: IPv4 router requirements](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812.html)

questions.prompt: A home-made packet parser always reads the TCP header starting at byte 20 of each IPv4 packet. Most packets decode correctly, but packets whose first byte is `0x46` (version 4, IHL 6) show nonsense port numbers. What is going wrong?

options.text: The parser ignores the IHL: these headers are 24 bytes long, so byte 20 is still inside the IPv4 options
options.explanation: Correct. IHL counts 4-byte words, so 6 means 24 bytes. The TCP header starts at byte 24; reading from byte 20 treats 4 bytes of options as the start of TCP.

options.text: IHL 6 means the packet is IPv6, so the whole layout differs
options.explanation: The first nibble, 4, is the version; the second nibble is the IHL. An IPv6 packet would start with version 6.

options.text: The Total Length field is wrong, so the payload is truncated
options.explanation: The Total Length field counts the whole datagram in bytes; nothing here suggests it is wrong. The fault is where the parser thinks the header ends.

options.text: IHL counts bytes, so the header is only 6 bytes and TCP starts at byte 6
options.explanation: IHL counts 4-byte words, not bytes, and no IPv4 header is shorter than 20 bytes (IHL 5).

questions.workedExample:
1. The first byte packs two 4-bit fields: version (4) and IHL (6).
2. IHL counts 4-byte words, so the header is 24 bytes: the fixed 20 bytes plus 4 bytes of options or padding.
3. The transport header begins where the IP header ends, at byte 24.
4. A parser that hard-codes 20 bytes reads the last 4 option bytes as TCP ports, so ports look random.
5. Fix: compute the header length from IHL on every packet (IHL 5 gives 20 bytes; the maximum, 15, gives 60).

questions.prompt: Why must an ordinary IPv4 forwarding router update the header checksum when it decrements TTL?

options.text: Because each link uses a different checksum algorithm
options.explanation: IPv4 uses one algorithm (the 16-bit ones' complement sum) everywhere. Link-layer checks like Ethernet's CRC are separate.

options.text: It doesn't; only the destination checks it
options.explanation: Every router verifies and regenerates the header checksum in IPv4.

options.text: Because the checksum covers the payload, which routers encrypt again
options.explanation: The IPv4 checksum covers the header, not payload. Ordinary forwarding does not encrypt the payload again.

options.text: Because the router decrements TTL, which changes the header
options.explanation: Correct. TTL is part of the checked header. The checksum must remain consistent after modification; an incremental update is sufficient.

questions.workedExample: TTL is in the IPv4 header, which is covered by the checksum. Forwarding changes TTL, requiring a checksum update, either incrementally or by recomputing. Other simultaneous header changes can also affect the checksum. IPv6 has no corresponding base-header checksum.

lessons.title: Parse a header and trace TTL
lessons.summary: Extract IPv4 header fields in Python and interpret a TTL difference only when its assumptions hold.
lessons.body:
The previous lesson described the header on paper. Here a short parser pulls the same fields out of real bytes, and the second half asks what the TTL field can and cannot tell you.

### Reading a header in Python

```python
import struct, socket

def parse_ipv4(pkt):
    # Header only; no payload validation.
    if len(pkt) < 20:
        raise ValueError("short header")
    # Split the first byte into two nibbles.
    version, ihl = pkt[0] >> 4, pkt[0] & 15
    if version != 4 or ihl < 5:
        raise ValueError("bad version/IHL")
    if len(pkt) < ihl * 4:
        raise ValueError("missing options")
    (vihl, tos, total, ident, ff,
     ttl, proto, csum, src, dst) = (
        # ! selects network byte order.
        struct.unpack("!BBHHHBBH4s4s",
                      pkt[:20]))
    if total < ihl * 4:
        raise ValueError("bad total length")
    return {
        "version": vihl >> 4,
        "ihl_bytes": (vihl & 0xF) * 4,
        "total_len": total,
        # Mask flags separately from offset.
        "DF": bool(ff & 0x4000),
        "MF": bool(ff & 0x2000),
        "offset": (ff & 0x1FFF) * 8,
        "ttl": ttl,
        "proto": proto,
        "src": socket.inet_ntoa(src),
        "dst": socket.inet_ntoa(dst),
    }

hdr = bytes.fromhex(
    "45000054abcd40004001bd1e"
    "c0a8010508080808")
print(parse_ipv4(hdr))
```

This prints version 4, a 20-byte header, total length 84, DF set, MF clear, offset 0, TTL 64, protocol 1 (ICMP), from `192.168.1.5` to `8.8.8.8`. This is a synthetic header illustrating a packet with an 8-byte ICMP header and 56 bytes of payload. Source address, identification, TTL and options depend on configuration; it is not a capture of a universal `ping` default. This parser extracts fields and validates basic lengths, but does not validate the checksum, option contents or complete payload.

## TTL: a hop budget

**Time To Live** is specified in seconds, but each forwarding router must decrement it by at least one. This also makes it a **hop-count limit**, without requiring a measurement of router queueing times.

If TTL reaches zero, the router discards the packet and normally sends ICMP **Time Exceeded**, subject to the rules suppressing errors for certain packets and to rate limiting.

Why bother? Transient routing loops can occur while routers disagree about the topology (see the interior routing lesson). Without TTL, forwarding has no hop-count expiry, though congestion or faults can still drop packets. With initial TTL at most 255 and compliant forwarding, an ordinary datagram cannot be forwarded indefinitely. Tunnel encapsulation uses its own outer TTL and needs separate consideration.

The sender chooses the initial TTL. If you know that starting value, and each router subtracts exactly one without rewriting or encapsulation, the amount that has gone missing counts the routers crossed: a packet sent with 64 that arrives with 52 passed 12 routers. Hosts and layer 2 switches do not decrement TTL; only forwarding routers do.

Both assumptions matter. An observed TTL alone does not establish the starting TTL, the path length or the sender's operating system, because the starting value is configurable and some devices rewrite TTL.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> A universal OS-default table and Internet hop-count range are omitted because they depend on platform versions, configuration and measurements not established here.

## Key takeaways
- The parser extracts fields and checks basic lengths, not checksum or payload validity.
- TTL is decremented by at least one by forwarding routers.
- A hop count follows from a TTL difference only with a known initial TTL and one decrement per hop.

## Further reading
- [RFC 791: Internet Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc791)
- [RFC 1812: IPv4 router requirements](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812.html)
- [Python struct module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html)

questions.prompt: Host A sends a packet with initial TTL 64 to host B. The path is A → switch → router R1 → router R2 → switch → B. All devices behave normally, with no TTL rewriting or tunnels. What TTL does B see, and why?

options.text: 62, because only the two routers decrement TTL
options.explanation: Correct. Forwarding routers decrement TTL; layer 2 switches forward frames without touching the IP header, and the sending and receiving hosts do not decrement it.

options.text: 60, because every device on the path decrements TTL
options.explanation: Switches work at layer 2 and do not change the IP header. Counting them, or the hosts, overstates the decrements.

options.text: 64, because TTL is only checked at the destination
options.explanation: Every forwarding router must decrement TTL; that is what limits a looping packet.

options.text: 63, because only the first router decrements it
options.explanation: Each router on the path decrements TTL, not just the first one.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify which devices forward at the IP layer: R1 and R2.
2. The switches forward Ethernet frames and leave the IP header alone.
3. A and B are the endpoints; they set and read TTL rather than decrementing it.
4. Two routers each take one off 64, so B sees 62.
5. Read in reverse, a TTL drop measures routers crossed only when you also know the starting value and that nothing rewrote it.

questions.prompt: A packet arrives with TTL 116. A colleague says: "That proves the sender runs Windows, which uses 128, so the packet crossed 12 routers." What is the sound response?

options.text: Agree: 128 − 116 is 12, so both conclusions follow
options.explanation: The subtraction is only meaningful if the starting value is known. An observed TTL cannot establish which value the sender chose.

options.text: Both claims rest on an unverified assumption: the starting TTL is configurable and devices can rewrite TTL, so 12 hops follows only if the start was really 128 with one decrement per router
options.explanation: Correct. TTL arithmetic gives a hop count only when the starting value and per-hop behaviour are independently known. It does not identify an operating system.

options.text: The packet crossed 116 routers
options.explanation: 116 is the value remaining, not the number of decrements.

options.text: TTL counts seconds, so the packet was 12 seconds old
options.explanation: Although the field was defined in seconds, routers in practice decrement it per hop; it does not measure elapsed time.

questions.workedExample:
1. A TTL difference counts hops only if you know the starting value and that each router subtracted exactly one.
2. The colleague infers the starting value from a guess about the operating system, then uses that guess to compute hops: both conclusions depend on the same assumption.
3. Senders can configure their initial TTL, and middleboxes or tunnels can change what you observe.
4. If you independently confirm a start of 128 and ordinary forwarding, then 12 routers follows. Otherwise, treat it as a hint, not proof.

lessons.title: How IPv4 fragments a datagram
lessons.summary: Explain how MTU, eight-byte offsets and the MF flag let a router split a DF-clear IPv4 datagram.
lessons.body:
Different links carry different maximum packet sizes. This lesson explains what an IPv4 router does when a datagram is too big for the next link, and how the destination puts the pieces back together.

## Fragmentation

An IP interface's **maximum transmission unit** (MTU) is the largest IP packet it supports without IP fragmentation. Link-specific mechanisms may fragment below IP. Basic Ethernet commonly uses 1,500 bytes. PPPoE plus PPP consumes 8 bytes within its Ethernet payload, giving 1,492 unless larger payload support is negotiated as in RFC 4638. Encapsulation reduces the inner MTU for a fixed outer path MTU.

If a router must forward a datagram bigger than the next link's MTU, IPv4 gives it two choices:

1. **Fragment** it into smaller datagrams, if the **DF** (Don't Fragment) flag is clear.
2. **Drop** it if DF is set, and report ICMP "Fragmentation Needed" when error-generation and rate rules permit.

In ordinary IP forwarding, reassembly is performed at the **destination**, not as a normal transit-router step. Firewalls/NATs may track or reassemble fragments for their separate functions, and a tunnel endpoint is the destination of the outer packet. Each fragment has its own IP header; option-copy rules mean not every option appears in every fragment. Fragments share the same **Identification field** value, carry an **offset** in 8-byte units and have **MF** set unless they contain the end of the original payload.

Fragment sizes follow from one constraint. The offset field counts in 8-byte units, so every fragment except the last must carry a multiple of 8 bytes of data. A router therefore fills each non-final fragment with as much data as fits after the header, rounded down to a multiple of 8, and writes each fragment's starting position divided by 8 into the offset field.

> [!example] Fragmenting 4,000 bytes over a 1,500-byte link
> A datagram has a 20-byte header and 3,980 bytes of data. Each fragment can carry 1,500 − 20 = 1,480 bytes of payload, which is already a multiple of 8.
>
> - Fragment 1: 1,480 bytes, offset 0, MF set
> - Fragment 2: 1,480 bytes, offset 185 (byte 1,480 ÷ 8), MF set
> - Fragment 3: 1,020 bytes, offset 370 (byte 2,960 ÷ 8), MF clear
>
> Check: 1,480 + 1,480 + 1,020 = 3,980. Total lengths on the wire are 1,500, 1,500 and 1,040.

The rounding matters when the room left is not a multiple of 8. An MTU of 1,000 leaves 980 bytes after a 20-byte header, but a non-final fragment can only use 976: a second fragment starting at byte 980 would need an offset of 122.5, which the field cannot express.

The destination collects fragments with the same source, destination, protocol and Identification, places each one at its offset, and knows it has the end when it sees a fragment with MF clear. Only when every gap is filled can it hand the datagram up.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Splitting a delivery across vans
> A removal firm has more boxes than one van can carry, so it loads several vans. Every van carries the same job number, a note saying where its boxes go in the sequence, and all but the last say "more vans coming". Only the destination house unpacks and reassembles the full load.
>
> **How it maps:** The job number is the Identification field, the sequence note is the fragment offset, "more vans coming" is the MF flag, and each van's own paperwork is the per-fragment IP header. Intermediate depots (routers) move vans without unpacking them.
>
> **Where it stops:** A real firm would resend one missing van. IP does not: if any fragment is lost, the whole datagram is abandoned and any recovery is left to TCP or the application. And unlike boxes, fragment payloads must be cut on 8-byte boundaries.

## Key takeaways
- Each fragment has an IP header; ordinary transit routers leave reassembly to the destination.
- Non-final fragment payloads must be multiples of eight bytes.
- Offsets count eight-byte units; MF is clear on the piece containing the payload end.
- The destination reassembles by Identification and offset; losing one fragment loses the datagram.

## Further reading
- [RFC 791: Internet Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc791)
- [RFC 8900: IP fragmentation fragility](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8900.html)
- [RFC 6864: IPv4 Identification](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6864)

questions.prompt: A home-made router splits a 2,000-byte IPv4 datagram (20-byte header, 1,980 bytes of data, DF clear) for a link with a 1,000-byte MTU. It sends fragments carrying 980, 980 and 20 bytes of data, each with a 20-byte header. Every destination rejects or misassembles the result. What is the design error?

options.text: It should have set DF so the datagram would not be fragmented
options.explanation: DF tells routers not to fragment; it would make the router drop the datagram, not fix its fragment sizes. The question is why these fragments are invalid.

options.text: Non-final fragments must carry a multiple of 8 bytes: the second fragment would start at byte 980, which the 8-byte offset field cannot express, so they should carry 976
options.explanation: Correct. 980 ÷ 8 is 122.5, which the offset field cannot hold. Using 976 bytes (the largest multiple of 8 that fits) puts every boundary on an 8-byte unit.

options.text: The last fragment is too small; every fragment must be the same size
options.explanation: Only non-final fragments are constrained. The last fragment carries whatever remains, however small.

options.text: Each fragment should carry the original header only once, in the first fragment
options.explanation: Every fragment is a complete IP datagram with its own header; that is how routers can forward fragments independently.

questions.workedExample:
1. The Fragment Offset field counts 8-byte units, so a fragment can only start at a byte position divisible by 8.
2. With a 980-byte first fragment, the second would start at byte 980, which is not divisible by 8.
3. The fix is to round the room after the header (980 bytes) down to 976 for every non-final fragment.
4. That gives 976, 976 and 28 bytes of data, starting at bytes 0, 976 and 1,952 (offset values 0, 122 and 244), with MF clear only on the last.
5. The last fragment is exempt from the multiple-of-8 rule because nothing follows it.

questions.prompt: For a normally fragmented IPv4 datagram with a complete transport header in its first fragment, and ordinary IP forwarding without middlebox reassembly, which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fragments are reassembled only by the destination host
options.explanation: Correct under the stated forwarding model. Firewalls, NATs and tunnel endpoints can have separate reassembly functions.

options.text: If one fragment is lost, only that fragment is retransmitted
options.explanation: IP has no fragment retransmission mechanism. Higher layers may recover the missing data, possibly repacketising it; IP does not itself resend the datagram.

options.text: Only the first fragment carries the TCP or UDP header
options.explanation: Correct under the stated first-fragment assumption. IPv4 otherwise permits tiny first fragments that do not hold the whole TCP header; later fragments lack a directly available port tuple.

options.text: All fragments of one datagram share the same Identification value
options.explanation: Correct. The destination groups fragments by (source, destination, protocol, Identification).

options.text: IPv6 routers fragment packets in the same way when needed
options.explanation: Incorrect. IPv6 routers never fragment; they drop the packet and send ICMPv6 Packet Too Big. Only the source host may fragment.

questions.workedExample: Ordinary forwarding preserves fragments until destination reassembly. IP does not retransmit a lost fragment. Under the specified layout the transport header is in the first fragment. Reassembly associates source, destination, protocol and Identification, then uses offsets/MF to reconstruct the payload. IPv6 routers do not perform IP fragmentation; only the source does.

lessons.title: Why fragmentation is fragile
lessons.summary: Explain fragment loss, reassembly state and Identification wrap-around, then contrast IPv6.
lessons.body:
Fragmentation lets an oversized IPv4 datagram cross a small-MTU link, but it creates problems that make networks and hosts avoid it where they can.

### Why fragmentation is avoided

Fragmentation works, but it is bad news in practice:

- **Loss amplification.** Lose any one fragment and the whole datagram is useless. IP itself has no fragment retransmission. Higher-layer or link-layer recovery is a separate mechanism.
- **The first fragment starts with the transport header.** A tiny first IPv4 fragment need not hold the complete TCP header. Later fragments normally lack ports, complicating stateless classification; stateful devices can associate fragments, while some policies drop them.
- **Reassembly costs memory** at the receiver and is a classic denial-of-service target (overlapping-fragment attacks, fragment floods).
- **ID wrap-around.** At high speeds the 16-bit Identification wraps quickly, risking fragments from different datagrams being stitched together.

How quickly? The field has 65,536 possible values. If a sender takes one per datagram to the same destination with the same protocol, the time before values repeat is simply 65,536 divided by the sending rate. At about 15,000 datagrams a second (roughly 8 KB datagrams at 1 Gbit/s) the counter wraps in about 4 seconds.

That is far shorter than reassembly state can last at a receiver (often tens of seconds). If a fragment of an old datagram is still waiting when a new datagram reuses its Identification value, the receiver can stitch pieces of two different datagrams together. The IPv4 header checksum does not cover the payload, and a transport checksum may not catch every such corruption.

IPv6 takes the lesson to heart: routers **never** fragment. Only the sending host may, using an extension header, and every IPv6 link must present an MTU of at least 1,280 bytes to IPv6, using fragmentation below IPv6 if the physical link needs it.

## Key takeaways
- Losing any fragment prevents reassembly of that datagram.
- Fragment handling consumes state and complicates filtering.
- A sequential Identification counter can repeat while old reassembly state remains; the rate and context matter.
- IPv6 routers do not fragment packets.

## Further reading
- [RFC 791: Internet Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc791)
- [RFC 8900: IP Fragmentation Considered Fragile](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8900.html)
- [RFC 6864: IPv4 Identification field](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6864)
- [RFC 8200: IPv6 Specification](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8200)

questions.prompt: A sender fragments every datagram and takes one value per datagram from a single 16-bit Identification counter for this source, destination and protocol. At its rate the counter wraps about every 4 seconds. The receiver keeps incomplete reassembly state for up to 30 seconds. One fragment of the datagram with ID 7 is lost. What risk follows?

options.text: A later datagram that reuses ID 7 can have its fragments combined with the stale leftover pieces, producing corrupted data
options.explanation: Correct. The leftovers of the old ID 7 are still held when the counter wraps, so fragments with matching source, destination, protocol and ID can be mis-assembled. Whether the receiver actually accepts the mixture depends on fragment layout and later checks.

options.text: None: TTL stops fragments from different datagrams being mixed
options.explanation: TTL limits forwarding hops; it does not label which datagram a fragment belongs to.

options.text: The receiver asks the sender to retransmit only the lost fragment
options.explanation: IP has no fragment retransmission. The incomplete datagram is eventually discarded; any recovery is up to TCP or the application.

options.text: No risk while the receiver's timeout is longer than the wrap time, because longer timeouts are always safer
options.explanation: It is the reverse: a reassembly timeout longer than the wrap time is what lets stale fragments meet a reused ID.

questions.workedExample:
1. A lost fragment leaves the rest of datagram ID 7 waiting at the receiver.
2. The counter wraps in about 4 seconds, so ID 7 is reused long before the 30-second state expires.
3. Fragments are grouped by source, destination, protocol and Identification, so pieces of the new and old datagrams can look like parts of one.
4. The IPv4 header checksum does not cover payload, so a mixed datagram is not automatically caught at the IP layer.
5. This is why RFC 4963 and RFC 6864 warn about high-rate fragmentation, and why protocols prefer to avoid fragmenting at all.

lessons.title: Path MTU and stalled transfers
lessons.summary: Trace MTU feedback, recognise a possible black hole and choose a TCP MSS clamp that fits a tunnel.
lessons.body:
Because fragmentation is fragile, modern senders try not to need it.

## Path MTU Discovery

The better approach is for the sender to learn the smallest MTU on the path (the **path MTU**) and send datagrams that fit. That is **Path MTU Discovery** (PMTUD, RFC 1191):

1. The sender sets **DF** on every packet and starts with its own link MTU.
2. A router that cannot forward a packet drops it and returns ICMP type 3, code 4 ("Fragmentation Needed and DF set"), which an RFC 1191 router fills with the next-hop MTU. Older messages may report zero and require fallback estimation.
3. The sender lowers its path estimate; retransmission or repacketisation depends on the transport/application. IP itself does not promise to resend.

```
Host        R1          R2        Server
 |  1500,DF  |           |           |
 |---------->|  1500,DF  |           |
 |           |---------->| MTU 1400! |
 |           |  ICMP 3/4 |           |
 |<----------------------| mtu=1400  |
 |  1400,DF  |           |           |
 |---------------------------------->|
```

IPv6 does the same with ICMPv6 **Packet Too Big**.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A lorry and a low bridge
> A haulier sends tall lorries along a route it has never driven. At a low bridge the lorry cannot pass, so the bridge keeper stops it there and sends a note to the depot: "maximum height 4 m on this road". The depot sends a fresh copy of that cargo in a lower lorry and uses lower lorries from then on.
>
> **How it maps:** The lorry height is the packet size, the low bridge is the smallest-MTU link, "stop, do not split the load" is the DF flag, and the note is the ICMP Fragmentation Needed or Packet Too Big message carrying the next-hop MTU. The stopped lorry is a dropped packet: nothing is sent back except the note, so any resending is done by the sender's transport, such as TCP, from its own copy.
>
> **Where it stops:** If the depot's post room bins the notes (a firewall blocking ICMP), the depot never learns and keeps sending tall lorries that silently disappear. Real networks can also recover without the note by probing with gradually larger packets, which has no tidy road equivalent.

### The PMTUD black hole

Classic ICMP-based PMTUD depends on error feedback reaching the sender. If that feedback is blocked and no effective probing/fallback recovers, a **black hole** can result: the TCP handshake works (small packets), but as soon as full-size data packets are sent, they vanish silently. Users see web pages that start loading and then hang.

Common fixes:

- **Permit necessary ICMP errors.** IPv4 type 3/code 4 and ICMPv6 type 2 carry MTU feedback. ICMPv6 also supports essential functions such as neighbour discovery; treat message types appropriately rather than applying a blanket rule.
- **MSS clamping.** Routers on tunnels or PPPoE links rewrite the TCP **MSS** (maximum segment size) option in SYN packets to limit what the receiving peer sends. Bidirectional coverage requires handling MSS advertisements in both directions; MSS is not one jointly negotiated value. MSS does not constrain UDP; senders must also account for any options when forming packets (RFC 6691).
- **Packetization Layer PMTUD** (RFC 4821, and RFC 8899 for datagram protocols like QUIC) probes with progressively larger packets and watches for loss, without relying on ICMP.

The MSS counts only TCP data, so the right clamp value is the MTU minus both the IP and TCP headers. For IPv4 and TCP without options that is 40 bytes: a 1,500-byte Ethernet MTU gives the familiar 1,460, and a 1,492-byte PPPoE link gives 1,452. A common mistake is to clamp to the link or tunnel MTU itself, which still lets full-size segments exceed it by 40 bytes.

IP or TCP options reduce the payload a sender can place in a packet of that MTU. RFC 6691 says the advertised MSS is calculated using the fixed headers, excluding options; the sender separately reduces actual payload to allow for the options it sends. Do not confuse that per-packet adjustment with changing the peer’s MSS advertisement.

## Key takeaways
- Classic PMTUD relies on permitted MTU feedback; symptoms alone do not prove an MTU fault.
- MSS advertisements limit TCP data in one direction and exclude IP/TCP headers.
- Encapsulation consumes packet room; PLPMTUD provides probing rather than depending on ICMP alone.

## Further reading
- [RFC 1191: Path MTU Discovery](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1191)
- [RFC 4821: Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4821)
- [RFC 6691: TCP options and MSS](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6691.html)
- [RFC 4638: Larger PPPoE MTUs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4638.html)
- [RFC 792: Internet Control Message Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc792)

questions.prompt: After a VPN change, small TCP exchanges work but larger transfers stall. The firewall blocks inbound ICMP. Which is a plausible cause to investigate, rather than a diagnosis established by these symptoms alone?

options.text: TCP's congestion window is too small
options.explanation: A small positive congestion window generally limits throughput. The packet-size pattern makes MTU handling worth investigating, but a capture is needed.

options.text: DNS is failing for large sites
options.explanation: A DNS problem does not directly explain a stall in an already established transfer to the same address.

options.text: The VPN encrypts traffic, which is too slow for large transfers
options.explanation: Encryption load can affect performance, but encryption alone does not establish why the size-dependent stall occurs.

options.text: A PMTUD black hole: full-size packets with DF set are dropped at the tunnel, and the ICMP 'Fragmentation Needed' replies never arrive
options.explanation: Correct as a hypothesis. If encapsulation makes packets too large, DF prevents fragmentation, ICMP feedback is blocked and probing does not recover, classic PMTUD can fail.

questions.workedExample: Check captures and interface/path MTUs to confirm whether oversized DF packets are dropped and whether corresponding ICMP errors reach the sender. Tunnel overhead matters relative to the actual outer MTU; not every tunnel has the same inner limit. Permit necessary MTU feedback, set a suitable interface MTU, or use appropriate TCP MSS/PLPMTUD support. TCP MSS adjustment must cover relevant directions and does not fix UDP. Retries can ultimately time out rather than continue forever.

questions.prompt: A GRE tunnel over IPv4 crosses an Ethernet path with a 1,500-byte MTU. GRE adds a 20-byte outer IPv4 header and a 4-byte GRE header, so the tunnel can carry inner IP packets of up to 1,476 bytes. An engineer clamps TCP MSS on SYNs in both directions to 1,476, but large transfers through the tunnel still stall while ICMP is blocked. Assume inner IPv4 and TCP without options. What is wrong with the clamp?

options.text: Nothing; the stall must be a congestion problem
options.explanation: With a correct clamp, full-size segments would fit. This clamp lets them exceed the tunnel MTU, which matches a size-dependent stall with blocked ICMP.

options.text: MSS counts only TCP data, so 1,476 bytes of data plus 40 bytes of inner IP and TCP headers makes 1,516-byte inner packets, too big for the tunnel; the clamp should be 1,436
options.explanation: Correct. Subtract the inner IP and TCP headers from the 1,476-byte tunnel MTU. Clamped at 1,436, the largest inner packet is exactly 1,476 bytes.

options.text: The clamp should be 1,460, the normal Ethernet value, because GRE overhead is added later
options.explanation: 1,460 ignores the 24 bytes of tunnel overhead, so full-size segments would still be too large for the tunnel.

options.text: MSS clamping only works on UDP, so it has no effect here
options.explanation: MSS is a TCP option; it does not apply to UDP at all. Here it applies, but with the wrong value.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate the layers: outer path 1,500 bytes; GRE overhead 24 bytes; tunnel MTU 1,476 bytes for the inner IP packet.
2. MSS limits TCP data only. Each inner packet also carries a 20-byte IP header and a 20-byte TCP header.
3. A 1,476-byte MSS therefore produces 1,516-byte inner packets: 40 bytes too many.
4. With ICMP blocked, the sender never learns of the drops, so large transfers stall while small exchanges work.
5. Clamp to 1,476 − 40 = 1,436 in both directions, and still allow the necessary ICMP so PMTUD works for other traffic such as UDP.

```
|outer IP 20|GRE 4|IP 20|TCP 20|data|
 <---------------- 1500 ----------->
```

lessons.title: Read ICMP and traceroute
lessons.summary: Interpret ICMP errors, ping replies and traceroute output without overclaiming what they prove.
lessons.body:
Interpret ICMP errors, ping replies and traceroute output without overclaiming what they prove.

## ICMP: IP's error and diagnostic channel

The **Internet Control Message Protocol** (ICMP, RFC 792) rides inside IP (protocol 1). Routers and hosts use it to report problems and answer probes. Each message has a **type** and a **code**:

| Type | Name | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Echo Reply | ping |
| 3 | Destination Unreachable | errors, PMTUD |
| 8 | Echo Request | ping |
| 11 | Time Exceeded | TTL expiry or reassembly timeout |

The IPv4 errors discussed here quote the offending IP header and at least the first 8 bytes of its payload, so the sender can match the error to the right connection (for a first fragment carrying TCP or UDP, these include the ports). The returned data cannot exceed what was actually available.

To avoid storms, hosts never send an ICMP error about an ICMP error, about a fragment other than the first, or about a broadcast. Routers also apply **rate limiting** to the ICMP they generate.

### ping

`ping` sends ICMP Echo Requests and measures reply **round-trip time**. A reply establishes that this probe/response exchange worked; it does not establish the health of the network application. A lost reply does not prove the host is down: many hosts and firewalls drop echo requests.

### traceroute: abusing TTL on purpose

`traceroute` discovers the routers along a path by sending probes with deliberately small TTLs:

1. Send a probe with a TTL of 1. The first router decrements it to 0, drops it and returns **Time Exceeded**. Its source address reveals hop 1.
2. Send with a TTL of 2. The second router replies. And so on.
3. Eventually a probe reaches the destination, which replies differently, and traceroute stops.

The classic Unix traceroute sends **UDP** probes to unlikely high ports (starting at 33434). The destination answers with ICMP **Port Unreachable** (type 3, code 3), which signals "you've arrived". Windows `tracert` sends ICMP Echo Requests instead and stops on an Echo Reply. Probe counts, starting ports and stopping rules depend on the implementation and options.

Illustrative output, not a live measurement:

```
$ traceroute example.net
 1  192.168.1.1     1.2 ms  1.0 ms  1.1 ms
 2  10.20.0.1       8.4 ms  8.1 ms  8.9 ms
 3  * * *
 4  203.0.113.9    15.3 ms 14.8 ms 15.0 ms
```

> [!warning] Reading traceroute honestly
> - `*` means no matching reply arrived before the timeout. The probe or reply may have been lost, filtered or rate-limited. Later replies show some probes got further, not that every packet took the same path or that forwarding is faultless.
> - Each displayed time is a round trip to the responding interface, including reply generation and the network reply path. Differences between hops do not isolate one link's delay.
> - Flow-preserving probes, such as Paris traceroute, reduce artefacts from per-flow load balancing. They cannot guarantee a fixed path through per-packet balancing or routing changes.

## Key takeaways
- ICMP types and codes distinguish errors and Echo probes.
- Error suppression and rate limits mean silence does not prove a forwarding failure.
- Traceroute uses increasing TTL values; its displayed times include the network reply path.

## Further reading
- [RFC 791: Internet Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc791)
- [RFC 792: Internet Control Message Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc792)
- [RFC 1191: Path MTU Discovery](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1191)
- [RFC 4821: Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4821)
- [IP fragmentation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IP_fragmentation)
- [Traceroute — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traceroute)

- [RFC 8900: IP Fragmentation Considered Fragile](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8900.html)
- [RFC 6864: IPv4 Identification field](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6864)
- [RFC 4638: Larger PPPoE MTUs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4638.html)
- [RFC 6691: TCP options and MSS](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6691.html)
- [RFC 1812: IPv4 router requirements](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812.html)

questions.prompt: Classic Unix `traceroute` sends UDP probes to high, unused ports. How does it know a probe has reached the destination itself rather than an intermediate router? Assume replies are permitted and delivered, and the destination really has no UDP socket bound to the probe port.

options.text: traceroute compares the reply's source address with a DNS lookup of the target
options.explanation: traceroute does compare addresses, but the stopping signal is the change of ICMP message type. A multi-homed host may even reply from a different address.

options.text: The destination replies with ICMP Time Exceeded with a special code
options.explanation: For these probes, forwarding TTL expiry produces Time Exceeded. At the destination the unused UDP port instead produces Port Unreachable; Time Exceeded also has a separate reassembly-timeout code.

options.text: The destination replies with ICMP Port Unreachable, because nothing listens on that port
options.explanation: Correct. A router reports Time Exceeded (type 11); the destination host, finding no process on the UDP port, returns Destination Unreachable, code 3 (port unreachable). That different message ends the trace.

options.text: The destination replies with a UDP packet echoing the probe
options.explanation: Nothing listens on the port, so there is no application to send UDP back. The reply is ICMP from the kernel.

questions.workedExample:
1. A probe sent with a small TTL, say 3, reaches the third router with TTL 1; that router decrements it to 0, drops it and sends **ICMP type 11** (Time Exceeded).
2. When TTL is large enough, the probe reaches the destination intact.
3. The destination's kernel finds no socket on the probe's destination port and returns **ICMP type 3, code 3** (Port Unreachable).
4. traceroute sees the different type and stops.
5. Windows `tracert` uses ICMP Echo probes instead and stops on an Echo Reply (type 0).

questions.prompt: Your traceroute shows `* * *` at hop 4, but hops 5 to 9 reply normally and the destination is reached with low latency. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Hop 4 is dropping all traffic, so the path is broken
options.explanation: Later probes reached further nodes, so the observations do not show that all traffic was blocked. Different probes can use different paths.

options.text: No reply was received for those probes; suppression, filtering or loss are possible, and later probes did reach further
options.explanation: Correct. Stars do not identify whether the probe or response was lost or suppressed, and do not prove a transit outage.

options.text: The destination is blocking traceroute
options.explanation: The trace includes a destination reply. Missing replies from intermediate probes do not, by themselves, establish that the destination blocks the traffic; filtering can depend on the probe and path.

options.text: There is a routing loop at hop 4
options.explanation: These observations do not establish a loop. Loops, routing changes and load balancing require additional evidence; repeated addresses are not a universal signature.

questions.workedExample: Each star means the reply deadline for one traceroute probe expired. A router may suppress or rate-limit Time Exceeded; either direction may filter or lose packets. Later replies show successful further reachability for other probes, which can follow different paths. They do not establish that forwarding at one device is entirely faultless or identify the cause of the missing reply.

questions.prompt: Which statements about how ordinary ICMPv4 errors are generated are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The error types discussed here quote the offending IP header and at least its first 8 payload bytes when available
options.explanation: Correct. The traditional format supports identifying the original packet. The quote can be longer and cannot contain bytes absent from the triggering packet.

options.text: A host never generates an ICMP error in response to an ICMP error message
options.explanation: Correct. Otherwise two hosts could bounce errors back and forth indefinitely.

options.text: Routers commonly rate-limit the ICMP messages they generate
options.explanation: Correct. Rate limiting protects resources and limits error traffic. Missing traceroute replies can also arise from filtering or loss; implementation is not universally a slow CPU path.

options.text: ICMP runs over UDP port 7
options.explanation: Incorrect. ICMP is carried directly in IP with protocol number 1. Port 7 is the old UDP/TCP echo service, unrelated to ping.

options.text: Blocking all ICMP improves security with no side effects
options.explanation: Blanket blocking can impair ICMP-based PMTUD and diagnostics. Some endpoints recover through packetisation-layer probing, so a black hole is not inevitable.

questions.workedExample: The covered errors quote the original header and initial payload, permitting matching when enough identifying data is available. ICMPv4 suppresses errors about errors and other prohibited cases such as non-initial fragments and broadcast/multicast traffic. Rate limiting can suppress responses. ICMPv4 is IP protocol 1, not UDP port 7. Necessary errors include IPv4 type 3/code 4 for classical PMTUD; ICMPv6 type 2 serves the corresponding IPv6 role.

lessons.title: Prefixes, masks and address counts
lessons.summary: Translate between a CIDR prefix, a contiguous mask and an IPv4 address count.
lessons.body:
An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number. We write it as four bytes in decimal, separated by dots: `192.168.10.77` is `11000000.10101000.00001010.01001101`.

An address together with a prefix length divides into a **network prefix** and remaining **host bits**. The address alone does not tell you the split. An interface can have several addresses, and forwarding tables may contain aggregated prefixes or /32 host routes. Aggregation reduces the need for individual-host entries.

Where the split falls is the whole subject of this lesson.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Street name and house number
> A postal address has a street part, which gets the letter to the right road, and a house number, which picks one door on it. Everyone on the same street shares the street part.
>
> **How it maps:** The network prefix is the street: routers use it to deliver to the right network. The host bits are the house number within it. Hosts that share a prefix are on the same "street" and normally deliver to each other directly, without a router.
>
> **Where it stops:** On a letter you can see where the street name ends. In IPv4 the boundary is invisible in the address itself; the prefix length or mask tells you where it falls, and it can sit in the middle of an octet. Moving the boundary by one bit halves or doubles every "street".

## From classes to CIDR

Originally the split was fixed by the first bits of the address (**classful** addressing):

| Historical class | First octet bit range | Prefix | Conventional host capacity |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0–127 | /8 | 16.7 million |
| B | 128–191 | /16 | 65,534 |
| C | 192–223 | /24 | 254 |

These bit ranges do not make every included network assignable: 0/8 and 127/8 have special meanings. For a single classful network needing 2,000 conventional host addresses, a Class C was insufficient while a Class B left about 97% of its capacity unused. Multiple Class C allocations were another possibility, at the cost of routing entries. CIDR addressed allocation granularity and aggregation.

**Classless Inter-Domain Routing** (CIDR, 1993; now RFC 4632) fixed both problems. The prefix can be **any length** from 0 to 32 bits, written after a slash. `192.168.10.0/26` means "the first 26 bits are the network". Allocations could now match need, and adjacent blocks could be summarised into one route.

## Subnet masks

A **subnet mask** is the same information written as an address: 1-bits for the prefix, 0-bits for the host part.

```
/26 = 11111111.11111111.11111111.11000000
    = 255.255.255.192
```

A contiguous subnet-mask octet can be 0, 128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254 or 255. Full 255 octets precede at most one partly filled octet; any later octets are 0. You do not need to memorise every row; the pattern matters more. Each step down the table adds one prefix bit and halves the block:

| Prefix | Mask (last octet) | Block size | Usable hosts |
|---|---|---|---|
| /24 | 0 | 256 | 254 |
| /25 | 128 | 128 | 126 |
| /26 | 192 | 64 | 62 |
| /27 | 224 | 32 | 30 |
| /28 | 240 | 16 | 14 |
| /29 | 248 | 8 | 6 |
| /30 | 252 | 4 | 2 |

The **block size** in the interesting octet is 256 minus the mask value. The relationship underneath the whole table is that every host bit doubles the number of addresses, so each extra prefix bit halves the block:

```formula essential
N = 2^(32 − p)
where
N: the number of addresses in the network, including the network and broadcast addresses
p: the prefix length, the number after the slash (/26 means p is 26); a whole number from 0 to 32. The remaining 32 − p bits are host bits, and the power of 2 doubles the count once per host bit
In words: a longer prefix leaves fewer host bits and a smaller block. A /26 has 64 addresses, a /25 twice as many (128), a /27 half as many (32), and a /20 has 4,096.
```

Notice the direction: a **bigger** prefix number means a **smaller** network. A /28 is smaller than a /24, not larger.

For conventional IPv4 subnets through /30, reserve the all-zero host pattern as the network address and the all-one pattern as directed broadcast. Subtracting those two gives the conventional usable-host capacity; special-purpose ranges and provider reservations can reduce assignability further. A /28 therefore has 16 addresses and conventionally 14 usable. Point-to-point /31s and single-address /32s follow different rules, taught in the VLSM unit.

To find the network an address belongs to, a host ANDs the address with the mask. With the same configured mask, equal results identify the same numerical subnet. Actual next-hop selection uses routes and policy; a subnet comparison alone does not prove layer 2 connectivity or exclude a more-specific route.

## Key takeaways
- An address alone does not identify its prefix length.
- CIDR permits any IPv4 prefix length from zero through 32.
- Each added prefix bit halves the address block; conventional host capacity reserves two addresses.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4632: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632)
- [RFC 1918: Address Allocation for Private Internets](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918)
- [RFC 3021: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on Point-to-Point Links](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3021)
- [Classless Inter-Domain Routing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classless_Inter-Domain_Routing)
- [Subnet — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subnet)
- [ipaddress module — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html)

- [RFC 3927: IPv4 link-local addressing](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3927.html)
- [RFC 6598: Shared address space](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6598.html)

questions.prompt: An office subnet is a /28. Its DHCP pool runs out once about 14 devices have joined. A manager proposes changing it to a /29 "because we need a bigger network". What will happen, and what would actually add room? Assume conventional IPv4 subnets that reserve the network and broadcast addresses.

options.text: A /29 doubles the addresses to 32, so it fixes the problem
options.explanation: A larger prefix number means fewer host bits. A /29 has 8 addresses, half of a /28's 16.

options.text: A /29 halves the subnet to 8 addresses (6 usable), making things worse; a /27 doubles it to 32 addresses (30 usable)
options.explanation: Correct. Each extra prefix bit halves the block and each bit removed doubles it. Shortening the prefix to /27 gives the room, provided the neighbouring /28 is free so the larger block stays aligned.

options.text: Prefix length only affects routing, not how many hosts fit
options.explanation: The prefix decides how many host bits remain, which directly sets how many addresses the subnet holds.

options.text: A /29 keeps 16 addresses but frees the two reserved ones
options.explanation: Changing the prefix changes the block size; it does not remove the network and broadcast reservation.

questions.workedExample:
1. The prefix length counts network bits; the remaining bits number hosts.
2. A /28 leaves 4 host bits: 16 addresses, 14 conventionally usable, which matches the pool running out.
3. A /29 leaves 3 host bits: 8 addresses. A bigger prefix number means a smaller network.
4. A /27 leaves 5 host bits: 32 addresses, 30 usable.
5. In practice the /27 must also start on a multiple of 32, so the change usually means renumbering or absorbing the adjacent /28.

lessons.title: Recognise IPv4 subnet boundaries
lessons.summary: Find where a subnet starts and ends, and use those boundaries to predict which addresses are on-link or reserved.
lessons.body:
Knowing where a subnet starts and ends lets you predict whether two hosts can talk directly, and spot an address that should never be assigned. A calculator or Python's `ipaddress` module will do the arithmetic; the point here is to recognise the boundaries.

## The recipe

For conventional IPv4 subnets through /30:

1. Find the **interesting octet**: the first mask octet below 255. It can be 0 for a byte-aligned prefix such as /24.
2. **Block size**: 256 minus the mask value in that octet.
3. **Network address**: round the interesting octet down to a multiple of the block size; octets to the right become 0.
4. **Broadcast address**: the network's value in that octet, plus the block size, minus 1; octets to the right become 255.
5. **Usable hosts**: everything strictly between them.

Subnets of one size tile the address space in aligned blocks, like rulers laid end to end: a /26 block always starts at .0, .64, .128 or .192, never at .50.

This conventional capacity excludes all-zero and all-one host fields. On an RFC 3021 point-to-point /31, both addresses are endpoints; a /32 names one address. The next unit examines those exceptions. Special address ranges and platform reservations can further reduce assignable addresses; the arithmetic is not an allocation policy.

### Worked example 1: 192.168.10.77/26

- Mask: 255.255.255.192. Interesting octet: the 4th.
- Block size: 256 − 192 = 64. Blocks start at 0, 64, 128, 192.
- 77 falls in the block starting at 64.

```
Network    192.168.10.64
First host 192.168.10.65
Last host  192.168.10.126
Broadcast  192.168.10.127
Hosts      62
```

### Worked example 2: 172.16.45.200/20

- /20 = 8 + 8 + 4, so the mask is 255.255.240.0. Interesting octet: the 3rd.
- Block size: 256 − 240 = 16. Blocks start at 0, 16, 32, 48 ...
- 45 falls in the block starting at 32 (32 to 47).

```
Network    172.16.32.0
First host 172.16.32.1
Last host  172.16.47.254
Broadcast  172.16.47.255
Hosts      4,094
```

The 4th octet doesn't matter here: it's entirely host bits, so it's 0 in the network and 255 in the broadcast.

That has a practical consequence. Inside this /20, addresses such as 172.16.33.0 and 172.16.40.255 are ordinary host addresses: they end in .0 or .255, but they are neither the first nor the last address of the block. Only 172.16.32.0 and 172.16.47.255 are reserved.

## Using the boundaries

- **Same subnet or not?** Two hosts with the same mask are on the same subnet only if both fall inside one block. 192.168.10.77/26 and 192.168.10.130/26 look close but sit in different blocks (.64–.127 and .128–.191), so with only connected routes and a default gateway, each sends to its gateway rather than directly.
- **Assignable or not?** Within a conventional subnet up to /30, only the first (network) and last (broadcast) addresses are reserved. An address outside the block cannot be used on that subnet at all.

## Key takeaways
- Find the first mask octet below 255 and use its block size.
- Round that address octet down to the aligned block start.
- Fill later octets with zero for the network and 255 for the broadcast; /31 and /32 require different treatment.
- In blocks larger than /24, addresses ending .0 or .255 can be ordinary hosts; only the block's first and last addresses are reserved.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4632: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632)
- [RFC 3021: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on Point-to-Point Links](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3021)
- [Subnet — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subnet)
- [ipaddress module — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html)

questions.prompt: Host A is `10.20.30.40/27` and host B is `10.20.30.70/27`. Both are plugged into the same switch and VLAN, there is no router, and each host has only its connected route plus a default gateway that does not exist. A cannot reach B. Why?

options.text: A /27 cannot hold more than 30 hosts, so B was rejected
options.explanation: Capacity is not the issue; there are only two hosts here. The issue is which block each address sits in.

options.text: A and B are in different /27 blocks (.32–.63 and .64–.95), so A treats B as off-link and sends to the missing gateway instead of ARPing for B
options.explanation: Correct. /27 blocks are 32 addresses wide and start on multiples of 32. Being on the same switch does not matter: A's routing decision uses its configured subnet.

options.text: 10.20.30.70 is the broadcast address of A's subnet
options.explanation: A's subnet is 10.20.30.32/27, whose broadcast is 10.20.30.63. .70 lies outside it altogether.

options.text: Hosts on the same switch always need a router between them
options.explanation: Hosts in the same subnet on one switch talk directly. These two are in different subnets.

questions.workedExample:
1. /27 means blocks of 32 addresses: .0–.31, .32–.63, .64–.95 and so on.
2. A (.40) is in .32–.63; B (.70) is in .64–.95.
3. A's only matching route for B is the default, so it tries to ARP for the gateway, not for B.
4. The gateway does not exist, so nothing is sent to B, even though both share a switch.
5. Fix: put both hosts in one block (for example renumber B into .33–.62) or provide a working router between the two subnets.

questions.prompt: A server is configured as `10.4.77.9/19`. A colleague wants to give another host on the same subnet one of these addresses. Which one can be assigned as an ordinary host address? Assume a conventional subnet with network and broadcast addresses reserved and no other reservations.

options.explanation: This is the last address of the block 10.4.64.0–10.4.95.255, so it is the subnet's broadcast address.
A /19 spans 32 values of the third octet. 77 sits in the block 64–95, so 10.4.96.1 belongs to the next subnet.
Correct. 10.4.80.0 lies inside 10.4.64.0–10.4.95.255 and is neither its first nor last address. Ending in .0 does not make it reserved in a block this large.
This is the first address of the block, so it is the network address.

questions.workedExample:
1. A /19 leaves the last 5 bits of the third octet and all of the fourth as host bits, so blocks are 32 wide in the third octet: 0–31, 32–63, 64–95, 96–127.
2. 77 falls in 64–95, so the subnet runs from 10.4.64.0 to 10.4.95.255.
3. Reserved: only 10.4.64.0 (network) and 10.4.95.255 (broadcast).
4. Outside: 10.4.96.1 is in the next block.
5. 10.4.80.0 is inside and is not the first or last address, so it is an ordinary host address.

lessons.title: Plan VLSM and point-to-point links
lessons.summary: Compare configured subnets, allocate aligned blocks and check /31 and /32 exceptions in Python.
lessons.body:
Real address plans mix subnet sizes. This lesson checks whether two hosts share a subnet, carves one block into right-sized pieces, and covers the /31 and /32 exceptions.

### Worked example 3: are they on the same subnet?

Host A is `10.0.0.130/25` and host B is `10.0.0.120/25`.

- /25 mask: 255.255.255.128, block size 128. Blocks: 0–127 and 128–255.
- A is in 10.0.0.128/25; B is in 10.0.0.0/25.

They are on **different** numerical subnets. With only connected subnet routes and a suitable gateway route, A sends to B via that gateway, even though the addresses look close. A wrong mask can cause partial connectivity, depending on the available routes and next-hop resolution.

### Worked example 4: carving up a /24 (VLSM)

You have `192.168.1.0/24` and need subnets for 100 hosts, 50 hosts, 20 hosts and two point-to-point router links. **Variable-length subnet masking** (VLSM) gives each subnet the smallest address block (longest prefix) that fits.

To size one subnet, pick the smallest block whose usable count covers the need: 100 hosts do not fit a /26 (62 usable) but do fit a /25 (126 usable). Leave headroom where growth is expected, because enlarging a subnet later usually means renumbering.

Doing that for each need, and starting at the aligned beginning of this unused /24, allocate largest first at the lowest available address:

| Need | Prefix | Range |
|---|---|---|
| 100 hosts | /25 (126) | .0 – .127 |
| 50 hosts | /26 (62) | .128 – .191 |
| 20 hosts | /27 (30) | .192 – .223 |
| link | /30 (2) | .224 – .227 |
| link | /30 (2) | .228 – .231 |

That leaves .232 – .255 free for later. Placing small subnets first can leave alignment gaps before later large blocks; the exact result depends on placement.

> [!tip] /31 and /32
> A /30 wastes half its four addresses on network and broadcast. On point-to-point links, RFC 3021 allows a **/31**: both addresses are endpoint addresses, with no directed broadcast. Limited broadcast (255.255.255.255) remains available. A **/32** names a single host and is used for loopback addresses and host routes.

### Let Python check you

```python
import ipaddress as ip

def describe(cidr):
    # Keep the prefix; clear the host bits.
    net = ip.IPv4Interface(cidr).network
    count = net.num_addresses
    usable = count
    if net.prefixlen < 31:
        usable -= 2
    return (net, net.netmask,
            net.broadcast_address,
            usable)

print(describe("172.16.45.200/20"))
# (IPv4Network('172.16.32.0/20'),
#  IPv4Address('255.255.240.0'),
#  IPv4Address('172.16.47.255'), 4094)
```

`ip.IPv4Interface` accepts an interface address with host bits. By contrast, `ip.ip_network` defaults to strict network parsing: passing `192.168.1.77/26` raises `ValueError`, because the supplied address is not the network start. Use an interface when describing a host, or explicitly pass `strict=False` when clearing host bits is your intent.


## Key takeaways
- Numerically close addresses can belong to different configured subnets.
- Choose the smallest block that meets each conventional host requirement.
- Allocate descending sizes from an unused aligned start to avoid unnecessary alignment gaps.
- An RFC 3021 /31 uses both addresses as endpoints; Python strict network parsing rejects host bits.

options.text: A /24 holds only 254 usable addresses, and leases are held while devices stay connected, so the pool runs out; a /23 (510 usable) is the smallest that fits

options.text: A /25 would fix it, because a longer prefix means more hosts
options.explanation: A longer prefix leaves fewer host bits: a /25 holds 126 usable, half of a /24.

options.text: A /9 is needed, because 500 needs 9 bits
options.explanation: Nine host bits are needed, so the prefix is 32 − 9 = 23. A /9 would be an enormous block of over 8 million addresses.

2. A /24 leaves 8 host bits: 256 addresses, 254 usable, so the pool is exhausted after about 254 devices.

options.text: Same subnet: deliver directly, since both start with 192.168.1

/26  10.0.0.0   - .63
/26  10.0.0.64  - .127
/27  10.0.0.128 - .159
/28  10.0.0.160 - .175

options.text: The link's two router addresses are 10.9.0.14 and 10.9.0.15
options.explanation: Correct. A /31 has 2 addresses, aligned on an even number: .14 and .15.

options.text: The link has no usable addresses, because 2 − 2 = 0
options.explanation: Incorrect. RFC 3021 treats both addresses as endpoint addresses on the point-to-point link; neither is reserved as a directed broadcast.

options.text: Using /31 instead of /30 halves the address space used for links
options.explanation: Correct. A /30 uses 4 addresses for 2 usable; a /31 uses 2.

options.text: 10.9.0.15 is the broadcast address of this link
options.explanation: Incorrect. On a /31 there is no directed broadcast; both addresses are host addresses.

options.text: 10.9.0.13/31 could be the other end
options.explanation: Incorrect. .13 belongs to the /31 .12–.13; a /31 always starts on an even address.

questions.workedExample:
1. A /31 has one host bit, so it holds two addresses and always starts on an even number: .12–.13, .14–.15 and so on.
2. 10.9.0.14/31 → {.14, .15}.
3. RFC 3021: on point-to-point links, both are endpoint addresses; there is no directed broadcast. Limited broadcast remains available.
4. Saving: a /31 uses 2 addresses where a /30 uses 4, so 1,000 links save 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 addresses.

lessons.title: Private, shared and link-local space
lessons.summary: Distinguish RFC 1918, CGN shared space and link-local addresses, including overlap risks.
lessons.body:
Distinguish RFC 1918, CGN shared space and link-local addresses, including overlap risks.

## Special and private ranges

Some special-purpose blocks are listed below. This is not a complete registry:

| Block | Purpose |
|---|---|
| 10.0.0.0/8 | Private (RFC 1918) |
| 172.16.0.0/12 | Private (RFC 1918) |
| 192.168.0.0/16 | Private (RFC 1918) |
| 100.64.0.0/10 | Shared address space, intended for CGN deployments |
| 127.0.0.0/8 | Loopback |
| 169.254.0.0/16 | Link-local |

**Private** RFC 1918 addresses can be routed within cooperating private networks. They are not globally reachable address space and should not be advertised into the public Internet. NAT is one way to reach public services; application proxies and gateways are alternatives. `172.32.0.1` lies outside RFC 1918, but being outside a private block alone does not prove an address is assigned or reachable.

**100.64.0.0/10** (RFC 6598) is distinct shared address space intended to reduce conflict with customers' RFC 1918 networks in CGN deployments. It cannot guarantee absence of overlap when other networks also use shared space.

**169.254.0.0/16** is IPv4 link-local space. Automatic assignment can occur when routable configuration is unavailable, but the presence of a link-local address alone does not prove a DHCP failure. RFC 3927 reserves the first and last /24 within this block from automatic selection, and routers must not forward link-local traffic to other links.

> [!warning] Overlapping private ranges
> Connecting networks with overlapping addresses can make destination-only routing ambiguous. Coordinate an address plan with connected organisations and cloud networks. Renumbering, translation or separate routing contexts can address different cases; choosing a supposedly unusual RFC 1918 block does not guarantee uniqueness.

## Key takeaways
- RFC 1918 has three specific private blocks; nearby addresses need not be private.
- Shared 100.64.0.0/10 space is distinct and cannot guarantee that interconnected networks never overlap.
- A link-local address does not by itself establish a DHCP failure.
- Overlapping destination addresses need an addressing or routing-context solution.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4632: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632)
- [RFC 1918: Address Allocation for Private Internets](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918)
- [RFC 3021: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on Point-to-Point Links](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3021)
- [Classless Inter-Domain Routing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classless_Inter-Domain_Routing)
- [Subnet — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subnet)
- [ipaddress module — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html)

- [RFC 3927: IPv4 link-local addressing](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3927.html)
- [RFC 6598: Shared address space](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6598.html)

Merely picking a less familiar private prefix does not guarantee no future overlap.
