lessons.title: Aggregate aligned routes
lessons.summary: Recognise when aligned prefixes can be summarised exactly and predict what an aggregate does to traffic.
lessons.body:
Every route a router advertises costs table space in every router that hears it. Summarising many prefixes into one keeps tables small, but changes which traffic a router attracts.

## Supernetting and route aggregation

CIDR's other half is **route aggregation** (also called **supernetting** or **summarisation**): advertising several contiguous networks as one shorter prefix.

Suppose an ISP has customers on `200.10.0.0/24`, `200.10.1.0/24`, `200.10.2.0/24` and `200.10.3.0/24`. Write the third octets in binary:

```
0 = 000000|00
1 = 000000|01
2 = 000000|10
3 = 000000|11
```

The first 22 bits match (16 from the first two octets, 6 here), so the ISP advertises one route: **200.10.0.0/22**. The rest of the Internet needs one entry instead of four.

The general rule: merging two equal, adjacent blocks takes one bit off the prefix, four take two bits, eight take three. So four /24s become a /22 and two /25s become a /24.

Aggregation requires **prefix alignment**. The block must start on a multiple of its size: to merge four /24s, the first one's number (here the third octet) must be a multiple of four. `200.10.1.0` to `200.10.4.0` is also four /24s, but no single /22 covers exactly them. The best summary is `200.10.1.0/24`, `200.10.2.0/23` and `200.10.4.0/24`:

```python
import ipaddress as ip

nets = [ip.ip_network(f"200.10.{i}.0/24")
        for i in range(1, 5)]
# Merge only adjacent, aligned prefixes.
print(list(ip.collapse_addresses(nets)))
# [200.10.1.0/24, 200.10.2.0/23,
#  200.10.4.0/24]  (reprs shortened)
```

Aggregation reduces entries advertised to other networks, saving routing/forwarding state. How a router stores control-plane and forwarding tables is implementation-dependent. A maintained aggregate can hide a component route's changes from upstream peers, depending on advertisement policy.

The catch is that a summary can attract traffic for addresses that don't exist, or that live elsewhere. A more-specific route wins by **longest-prefix match**, but only if it exists. An aggregate can still attract traffic for unavailable destinations. The advertising router needs appropriate component routes and discard handling for unmatched portions to avoid forwarding loops.

For example, a router that advertises 10.1.0.0/21 but only has routes for 10.1.4.0/22 attracts traffic for 10.1.0.0 to 10.1.3.255 too. With no more-specific route for those addresses, it either discards them (with a discard or "null" route for the aggregate) or, if its own default route points back towards the sender, bounces them in a loop until TTL expires.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Telephone area codes
> A caller abroad does not need a list of every London subscriber. Their phone network only needs "numbers starting +44 20 go to the London exchange". The London exchange holds the detailed list.
>
> **How it maps:** The area code is the aggregate prefix; the detailed subscriber list is the set of more-specific routes held only by the router that summarises them. Distant routers keep one entry instead of thousands.
>
> **Where it stops:** A call to an unassigned London number still travels to the London exchange before it fails, just as an aggregate attracts traffic for unused addresses. And unlike area codes, prefixes can only be summarised when the blocks are numerically aligned on a power-of-two boundary.

## Address exhaustion

IPv4 has 2³² possible address values (32 copies of 2 multiplied together: 4,294,967,296, about 4.3 billion), and special-purpose ranges reduce the pool available for globally unique assignments. Address sharing, transfers and allocation policies address scarcity in different ways; IPv6 provides a much larger address space.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> Current global route counts, address-market prices and a regional exhaustion/allocation timeline are absent because they require dated measurements and registry-policy evidence not established in this lesson. No universal purchase price or route-memory design is assumed.

## Key takeaways
- Exact aggregation requires contiguous, correctly aligned blocks.
- A larger covering route can attract traffic for unavailable component destinations.
- More-specific installed routes win; discard handling can prevent loops through aggregate gaps.
- IPv4 scarcity concerns usable allocations, not only the raw 32-bit value count.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4632: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632)
- [Classless Inter-Domain Routing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classless_Inter-Domain_Routing)
- [ipaddress module — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html)

questions.prompt: Branch router B has routes for `10.1.4.0/24` through `10.1.7.0/24` only. To keep things simple it advertises the summary `10.1.0.0/21` to the core. B's own default route points to the core, and B has no discard route for the summary. A core router forwards a packet for 10.1.2.9 to B. What happens?

options.text: B delivers it, because the summary covers 10.1.2.9
options.explanation: The summary only advertises reachability; B still needs a specific route. It has none for 10.1.0.0 to 10.1.3.255.

options.text: B's longest match is its default route, so it sends the packet back to the core, which sends it to B again: a loop until TTL expires
options.explanation: Correct. The /21 is eight /24s, so it claims 10.1.0–3 that B does not have. Without a discard route for the aggregate, B's default sends the traffic back up. Advertising the exact 10.1.4.0/22, or adding a discard route, avoids this.

options.text: The core rejects the summary because 10.1.0.0/21 is not aligned
options.explanation: 10.1.0.0/21 is a valid aligned prefix. The problem is that it covers more than B actually has.

options.text: Nothing changes, because aggregation never affects which router receives traffic
options.explanation: Advertising a covering prefix is exactly what attracts traffic for every address inside it.

questions.workedExample:
1. 10.1.0.0/21 covers third octets 0 to 7; B only has 4 to 7, which together form the aligned block 10.1.4.0/22.
2. The core follows the /21 to B for 10.1.2.9.
3. On B, no specific route matches, so its longest match is the default via the core.
4. The packet bounces between core and B until TTL runs out.
5. RFC 4632's rule: a router that originates an aggregate must discard packets that match it but none of its more-specific routes, normally with a discard (null) route for the aggregate. Better still, advertise exactly 10.1.4.0/22.

questions.prompt: Which of these pairs can be summarised **exactly** by one prefix? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. 0 and 1 differ only in the last bit of the third octet, and 0 is aligned for a /23: 192.168.0.0/23.
Incorrect. They're contiguous but not aligned: a /23 must start on an even third octet, so 1–2 straddles two /23s (0–1 and 2–3).
Correct. The two halves of 10.0.0.0/24 combine into that /24.
Correct. 8–11 and 12–15 together are 8–15, a block of 8 starting at 8, which is aligned: 172.16.8.0/21.
Incorrect. Together they cover 2–5, but a /22 must start at a multiple of 4 (0 or 4), so no single prefix matches.

questions.workedExample:
Rule: two equal-size blocks merge into one prefix only if they're **adjacent** and the lower one starts on a multiple of **twice** their size.

1. /24s at 0 and 1: pair size 2, 0 is a multiple of 2 ✓ → /23.
2. /24s at 1 and 2: 1 isn't a multiple of 2 ✗.
3. /25s at 0 and 128: pair size 256, 0 ✓ → /24.
4. /22s at 8 and 12: pair size 8, 8 is a multiple of 8 ✓ → /21.
5. /23s at 2 and 4: pair size 4, 2 isn't a multiple of 4 ✗.

Python's `ipaddress.collapse_addresses` returns one network for exactly the valid cases.

lessons.title: Translate ports and expire mappings
lessons.summary: Trace a NAPT translation table and distinguish mapping reuse, filtering and idle expiry.
lessons.body:
IPv4 has 2³² possible address values (32 copies of 2 multiplied together), about 4.3 billion, with some reserved for special purposes. **NAT** shares or translates address space; **IPv6** provides a much larger address space. They address different aspects of connectivity and coexist in deployed networks.

## Network address translation

A **NAT** device, usually your home router or a cloud NAT gateway, sits between a private network and the Internet. It rewrites addresses in packets as they pass through, so many private hosts can share one or a few public addresses.

### Kinds of NAT

- **Static NAT**: a fixed one-to-one mapping. Private 10.0.0.5 always appears as public 198.51.100.5. Used to expose a server.
- **Dynamic NAT**: private hosts borrow a public address from a pool while they're active. Still one private address per public address at any moment.
- **NAPT / PAT** (port address translation, often called "NAT overload" or masquerading): many private hosts share **one** public address, distinguished by **port**. NAPT is commonly used on home gateways; product configurations differ.

### How port translation works

When a laptop at `192.168.1.10:51000` opens a connection to a web server, the router:

1. Selects a public address/port mapping, for example port 40000. Allocation and possible reuse depend on protocol and mapping policy.
2. Records a mapping in its translation table.
3. Rewrites the source to `203.0.113.7:40000`, updates the IPv4 header checksum and the TCP checksum (or a nonzero UDP checksum), and forwards. An IPv4 UDP zero checksum means no checksum was supplied and remains zero.
4. When the reply arrives for `203.0.113.7:40000`, looks up the mapping, rewrites the destination back to `192.168.1.10:51000` and forwards it inside.

```
inside              NAT        outside
192.168.1.10:51000 --+
                     | 203.0.113.7:40000
192.168.1.11:51000 --+ 203.0.113.7:40001
                     |
        table: (priv ip, port) <-> pub port
```

The heart of NAPT is its translation table. After the two laptops above open connections, a simplified table for one protocol and one public address looks like this:

| Inside endpoint | Public endpoint |
|---|---|
| 192.168.1.10:51000 | 203.0.113.7:40000 |
| 192.168.1.11:51000 | 203.0.113.7:40001 |

Both laptops happen to use source port 51000, so the router gives them different public ports to tell their replies apart. A reply to 203.0.113.7:40001 matches the second row and goes to 192.168.1.11. An unsolicited packet to 203.0.113.7:8080 matches no row, so in this simple model it is dropped: there is nobody inside to send it to.

Real routers can add rows deliberately, with static mappings (port forwarding), a configured fallback host or services listening on the router itself. Translation lookup and firewall policy are distinct functions.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: An office switchboard
> An office has one public phone number. When a member of staff makes an outside call, the receptionist notes "line 40000 is extension 10's call" so that when the other party rings back on that line, the call is put through to the right desk. An unexpected call on a line nobody has used gets no answer.
>
> **How it maps:** The public number is the shared public IP address, the lines are public ports, the extensions are private addresses and ports, and the receptionist's notebook is the translation table. Entries made by outgoing calls are dynamic mappings; a standing instruction to put all calls on one line through to the sales desk is a static port forward.
>
> **Where it stops:** A receptionist does not rewrite anything, whereas a NAT changes addresses, ports and checksums in every packet. NAT entries also expire after idle periods, and some NATs accept a return call only from the exact party that was called, which is a filtering rule rather than part of the mapping.

Real NATs expire state. RFC 4787 requires UDP mappings to last at least two idle minutes, with a specific exception for certain well-known destination ports; it recommends a default of at least five minutes. RFC 5382 specifies at least 2 hours 4 minutes for idle established TCP connections when the NAT cannot determine whether endpoints remain active. These are protocol requirements, not measurements of every router. Keepalive choices must account for the application, state-refresh rules and actual network.

### Separate mapping reuse from inbound filtering

NATs differ in two ways that matter for peer-to-peer apps (RFC 4787 terms):

| Behaviour | Endpoint-independent | Address-and-port-dependent |
|---|---|---|
| Mapping | Reuses a mapping for the same internal endpoint across destinations | Mapping depends on the remote IP and port |
| Filtering | Anyone may send to the mapping | Only previously contacted remote IP:port pairs |

Older literature uses "full cone", "restricted cone", "port-restricted cone" and **symmetric NAT**. Those historical categories combine properties; describing mapping reuse and inbound filtering separately is clearer. Destination-dependent mapping can make a STUN-observed mapping unusable with another peer. It does not by itself prove that all direct connectivity checks will fail.

## Key takeaways
- NAPT can share a public address by translating transport ports.
- An inbound packet with no matching mapping has no inside destination unless a static rule exists.
- Mapping reuse and inbound filtering describe different properties.
- Idle-state requirements differ by protocol; application keepalives need the actual refresh rules.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4787: NAT Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4787)
- [RFC 5382: NAT Behavioral Requirements for TCP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5382)
- [Network address translation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_address_translation)

questions.prompt: A home router doing NAPT has public address 203.0.113.7. Its translation table holds two mappings, public ports 40000 and 40001. A packet arrives from the Internet for `203.0.113.7:8080`, and nobody has set up port forwarding. What does the router do? Use the lesson's simple one-protocol translation-table model: no local service, fallback host or other inbound rule.

options.text: Broadcasts it to every host on the LAN so the right one can answer
options.explanation: The stated model has no broadcast fallback: it only follows an existing mapping.

options.text: Forwards it to the host that most recently made an outbound connection
options.explanation: There's no such fallback. Guessing would send traffic to the wrong machine; the router has no mapping, so it has no destination.

options.text: Drops it, because no mapping exists for port 8080
options.explanation: Correct under the specified model. Real translation keys and local-service handling can be more complex than this port-only lookup.

options.text: Creates a new mapping for port 8080 and forwards it to the router's own web interface
options.explanation: The scenario excludes a local service or configured rule for that port. An unmatched arrival does not allocate an internal destination in this model.

questions.workedExample: For the fixed public address and single transport protocol, look up port 8080. Only 40000 and 40001 exist, so no row matches and the packet is dropped. Real routers may separately have local services, static mappings, filtering or fallback rules; those are explicitly excluded here.

questions.prompt: A VoIP app uses UDP behind IPv4 NAPT. Incoming calls fail after idle periods. A capture and NAT-state inspection confirm that the relevant mapping expires before the incoming request. Which response addresses this confirmed cause?

options.text: Use protocol-appropriate keepalives and/or adjust the permitted NAT policy based on the measured timeout and refresh behaviour
options.explanation: Correct. Outbound traffic can refresh the mapping, subject to NAT behaviour. Choose timing from evidence and protocol requirements, rather than assuming one universal consumer-router timer.

options.text: The server's DNS TTL expires; lower it to 30 seconds
options.explanation: Changing a DNS TTL does not refresh the confirmed expired translation mapping.

options.text: UDP is unreliable, so incoming packets are lost randomly; switch to TCP and nothing else
options.explanation: Switching transport alone does not guarantee state will remain available; TCP state can also expire and application/server state matters.

options.text: The phone's IPv6 temporary address rotated; disable privacy extensions
options.explanation: This is a confirmed IPv4 translation-state failure, not an IPv6 address-lifetime diagnosis.

questions.workedExample: The observation establishes that the mapping disappeared, rather than merely suggesting it from idle-time symptoms. Check which packets refresh the mapping and coordinate application keepalives or allowed NAT policy accordingly. RFC 4787 specifies a two-minute minimum UDP timer with a defined exception, but its requirement is not evidence of the timer on this device. Registration expiry and other server state still require separate handling.

lessons.title: NAT reachability and ICE traversal
lessons.summary: Explain NAT constraints and follow STUN, TURN and ICE through a connection attempt.
lessons.body:
Explain NAT constraints and follow STUN, TURN and ICE through a connection attempt.

## Why NAT breaks end-to-end connectivity

IP was designed so any host could send a packet to any other. NAT breaks that:

- **Inbound reachability needs a usable mapping and permitted traffic.** Static forwarding, mapping-control protocols, traversal or relays can provide it; a previously unused private endpoint is not automatically reachable through dynamic NAPT. Running a server, a game host or a video call at home becomes awkward.
- **Addresses in payloads break.** Protocols that carry IP addresses inside the data (FTP's active mode, SIP for VoIP) send the private address, which is useless outside. Some devices provide **ALGs** (application-level gateways) that rewrite protocol fields. Application-aware traversal and relays are alternatives; encryption or protocol differences can prevent an ALG from doing the required rewrite.
- **State in the middle.** Losing an active dynamic mapping can interrupt a connection. Replicated or recoverable state and static mappings change failure behaviour; not every NAT deployment is a single unrecoverable point of failure.
- **Carrier-grade NAT** shares public IPv4 addresses among subscribers. It can add another translation layer beyond a home NAT, and RFC 6598 provides 100.64.0.0/10 for shared internal addressing. Sharing ratios vary. IP-based bans can affect unrelated subscribers; attribution needs sufficiently detailed mapping records, including protocol, ports and time. A subscriber mapping is not proof of an individual person's identity.

> [!note] NAT is not a firewall
> Translation does not define a complete security policy. Missing mappings can prevent delivery, while filtering determines which traffic may use existing mappings. IPv6 can apply stateful firewall rules without network address translation.

## Application NAT traversal: STUN, TURN and ICE

Video calls, WebRTC, games and VPN meshes (Tailscale, for example) want direct peer-to-peer paths. Three protocols, used together, make that work:

**STUN** (RFC 8489): a client sends a request to a public STUN server, which replies "I saw you as 203.0.113.7:40000". The client now knows its **server-reflexive** address. Endpoint-independent mapping can make that address reusable with other peers, but filtering, mapping lifetime and path reachability still determine whether traffic works.

**UDP hole punching**: both peers learn their reflexive addresses via STUN, swap them through a signalling server, then send connectivity probes towards one another. This can create mappings and filtering state that permit replies. Exact simultaneity is unnecessary, and NAT/filter behaviour can still prevent success.

**TURN** (RFC 8656): when direct connectivity checks fail, a peer can allocate a reachable **relay** address; one or both peers may use relayed candidates. It can provide connectivity when direct paths fail, but the relay must be reachable and have capacity and valid credentials. Firewalls and network failures can still block it. Relaying costs bandwidth and can add latency.

**ICE** (RFC 8445) is the procedure that ties them together:

1. **Gather candidates**: host addresses (local interfaces), server-reflexive (from STUN) and relayed (from TURN).
2. **Exchange** candidates through signalling. WebRTC can include candidates in SDP descriptions and convey additional candidates later using Trickle ICE.
3. **Connectivity checks**: try candidate pairs in priority order with STUN requests.
4. **Nominate** a valid pair under ICE priorities and application policy. A direct pair is commonly preferred, but relays can be deliberately preferred and nomination does not benchmark every path for optimal performance.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Two callers behind switchboards
> Two people each sit behind an office switchboard and want to talk directly. Each first rings a friend outside and asks "what number did my call come from?", then they swap those numbers through a mutual contact and both dial at about the same time, so each receptionist sees the other's call as expected. If the switchboards still refuse, they both dial into a conference bridge instead.
>
> **How it maps:** Asking the outside friend is a STUN request revealing the server-reflexive address; the mutual contact is the signalling server; dialling at once is hole punching through connectivity checks; the conference bridge is a TURN relay; working through the options in order and settling on one that connects is ICE.
>
> **Where it stops:** A switchboard that gives each outside call a different line (destination-dependent mapping) makes the number your friend saw useless to anyone else, which phone systems rarely do. And ICE works through many candidate pairs in priority order, with several checks in flight, rather than strictly one call at a time.

```
         signalling server
          /             \
   Peer A ---- direct? ---- Peer B
     |   (hole punched)     |
     +------ TURN relay ----+
```

## Key takeaways
- NAT translation and firewall policy are different functions.
- Payload addresses, lost mapping state and shared addresses complicate applications and attribution.
- STUN discovers an observed mapping; it does not prove peer reachability.
- ICE checks candidate pairs and may use a TURN relay when direct checks fail.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4787: NAT Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4787)
- [RFC 8445: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8445)
- [RFC 8200: IPv6 Specification](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8200)
- [RFC 4862: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4862)
- [RFC 8305: Happy Eyeballs Version 2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8305)
- [Network address translation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_address_translation)
- [IPv6 adoption statistics — Google](https://www.google.com/intl/en/ipv6/statistics.html)

questions.prompt: Peer A's NAT uses address-and-port-dependent mapping AND filtering. After a successful STUN request over UDP, the server sees A as `198.51.100.4:50123`, but A's mapping towards Peer B uses a different port. All direct ICE candidate checks fail, while an authenticated TURN-relayed candidate succeeds. What explains the STUN candidate failure and the usable alternative?

options.text: STUN gave a wrong address because STUN only works over TCP; ICE retries STUN over TCP
options.explanation: STUN supports multiple transports; in this scenario it correctly reports the mapping observed by that server. It does not promise that mapping is usable by B.

options.text: The STUN-observed mapping is not a usable path for B under these mapping/filtering rules; ICE can nominate the working relayed candidate
options.explanation: Correct. The assumptions specify a distinct mapping and a separate filtering policy. Destination-dependent mapping alone would not prove that every direct path fails.

options.text: B needs to use IPv6; ICE switches B to IPv6
options.explanation: Address family isn't the issue. The mapping behaviour of A's NAT is.

options.text: The NAT drops all UDP; ICE falls back to port forwarding via UPnP
options.explanation: The successful STUN exchange contradicts a blanket UDP block in this scenario. ICE checks gathered candidates; an external mapping-control mechanism is separate.

questions.workedExample: The NAT allocated a mapping for the STUN destination and filters that mapping to its permitted peer. A different B mapping therefore cannot be reached merely by reusing the server-observed address. The question explicitly says all direct checks fail and a relayed check succeeds, so ICE can use that valid relay pair. NAT classification alone is insufficient to infer this outcome for every topology.

questions.prompt: Which of these are genuine problems caused by NAT or carrier-grade NAT? Select all that apply.

options.text: Private addresses embedded in SIP or active FTP payloads may be unusable by an external peer
options.explanation: Correct. A header-only translation does not repair embedded addresses. Application traversal, relays or suitable ALGs may handle them.

options.text: Banning one abusive IP behind CGNAT can block many innocent customers
options.explanation: Correct. Multiple subscribers can share a public address, so an address-wide restriction can affect unrelated subscribers; the sharing ratio is deployment-specific.

options.text: NAT encrypts traffic, so intrusion detection systems can't inspect it
options.explanation: NAT rewrites headers; it doesn't encrypt anything. Payloads are as visible as before.

options.text: Losing unsynchronised dynamic NAT state can interrupt existing connections
options.explanation: Correct. Active return mappings may disappear. Replication, preserved state or static mappings can alter this behaviour.

options.text: Attributing shared-address traffic to a subscriber needs mapping records with enough protocol, port and time detail
options.explanation: Correct. A public address alone can represent several subscribers. Required fields depend on the mapping policy; records do not prove which individual person sent traffic.

questions.workedExample: Embedded addresses can need application-aware handling. Shared public addresses complicate address-based blocking and subscriber attribution. Dynamic translation state introduces failure and expiry cases. NAT by itself rewrites addressing rather than encrypting application data. The relevant outcomes depend on configuration, state management and logging detail.

lessons.title: IPv6 headers and address notation
lessons.summary: Read IPv6 address forms and types, and contrast its base header and fragmentation rules with IPv4.
lessons.body:
IPv4's address shortage drove both NAT and IPv6. This lesson covers what is different about IPv6 packets and how to read its much longer addresses.

## IPv6

IPv6 (RFC 8200) is the long-term fix: **128-bit** addresses. Every extra bit doubles the number of possible addresses, so 96 more bits than IPv4 make an enormous difference: about 4.3 billion IPv4 address values against about 340 undecillion (34 followed by 37 zeros) for IPv6. Scarcity of addresses stops being the design constraint; the practical question becomes how to number and route subnets sensibly.

The base header is a fixed 40 bytes with no checksum; TTL is renamed **Hop Limit**, and extras go in optional extension headers.

IPv6 routers **never fragment**. A router that cannot forward a packet because it exceeds the next link's MTU drops it and sends ICMPv6 **Packet Too Big**, carrying that MTU, back to the source (subject to ICMPv6 rate limits). Only the source may fragment, using a Fragment extension header. Every IPv6 link must carry packets of at least 1,280 bytes, so a sender that keeps packets within that size can avoid relying on path MTU feedback.

### Writing addresses

Eight groups of four hex digits. Two rules shorten them (RFC 5952 gives the canonical form):

1. Drop leading zeros in each group.
2. Replace the **longest** run of at least two all-zero groups with `::`, once only (if runs tie, the first). RFC 5952 canonical output does not compress a single zero group.

```
2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329
2001:db8::ff00:42:8329

2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:1
2001:db8::1:0:0:1
```

### Address types

| Prefix | Type |
|---|---|
| 2000::/3 | Main global-unicast allocation block, including special-use subranges |
| fe80::/10 | Link-local |
| fc00::/7 | Unique local (ULA) |
| ff00::/8 | Multicast |
| ::1/128 | Loopback |

There is no broadcast; multicast groups like `ff02::1` (all nodes on the link) replace it. IPv6 addressing specifies a **link-local** address on each interface, apart from exceptions such as the loopback interface. An interface need not have a global address; multiple addresses are supported. `2001:db8::/32` in these examples is documentation space, not a publicly routed allocation. ULA local generation uses `fd00::/8`; the `fc00::/8` half is not defined for that method.

## Key takeaways
- IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and a fixed 40-byte base header.
- Canonical notation compresses the first longest run of at least two zero groups.
- IPv6 has multicast rather than broadcast and supports multiple addresses per interface.
- A router drops an oversized IPv6 packet and reports Packet Too Big when permitted.

## Further reading
- [RFC 8200: IPv6 Specification](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8200)
- [RFC 5952: IPv6 Address Text Representation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5952)
- [RFC 4291: IPv6 Addressing Architecture](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4291)
- [IPv6 address — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPv6_address)

questions.prompt: What is the canonical shortened form of `2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001`?

options.explanation: Correct. Drop leading zeros in each group (0db8 becomes db8, 0001 becomes 1) and replace the single run of five zero groups with `::`.
This is valid but not shortest. RFC 5952 says the longest run of zero groups must be compressed with `::`.
The `::` is right, but leading zeros in a group must also be removed in canonical form, so 0001 becomes 1.
Only *leading* zeros can be dropped. Removing the zeros inside 2001 changes the value of the group.

questions.workedExample:
1. Remove leading zeros: `2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1`.
2. Groups 3 through 7 are five zero groups.
3. Compress that longest run: `2001:db8::1`.
4. Expanding gives two initial groups, five zero groups and the final 1: eight groups total.

questions.prompt: `ip -6 addr` on a laptop shows `fe80::4a1f:2cff:fe9a:10b3/64`. What kind of address is this?

options.text: A global unicast address assigned by the ISP
options.explanation: The fe80::/10 prefix is link-local, not an ISP global-unicast allocation. Global unicast has more nuance than a single exhaustive 2000::/3 type test.

options.text: A unique local address (the IPv6 version of 10.0.0.0/8)
options.explanation: Unique local addresses are fc00::/7 (in practice fd00::/8). fe80:: is different.

options.text: A multicast group address
options.explanation: Multicast addresses start with ff (ff00::/8).

options.text: A link-local address, valid only on that one link
options.explanation: Correct. Routers must not forward packets with link-local source or destination onto other links.

questions.workedExample:
Match the prefix against the table:

| Prefix | Type |
|---|---|
| 2000::/3 | Main global-unicast allocation block |
| fe80::/10 | Link-local |
| fc00::/7 | Unique local |
| ff00::/8 | Multicast |

The address starts `fe80`, so it's **link-local**. The `ff:fe` in the middle is compatible with a MAC-derived modified EUI-64 identifier, but does not prove how it was generated.

questions.prompt: A router receives a 1,600-byte IPv6 packet that must go out over a link with a 1,500-byte MTU. What happens?

options.text: The router fragments it into two packets using the Fragment extension header
options.explanation: In IPv6 only the *source* host may fragment, using the Fragment header. Routers never fragment.

options.text: The router truncates the packet to 1,500 bytes and forwards it
options.explanation: IP never truncates payloads; that would silently corrupt data.

options.text: The router drops it and sends ICMPv6 Packet Too Big back to the source, with the MTU of 1,500
options.explanation: Correct for the stated ordinary forwarding case, subject to ICMPv6 generation/rate rules. IPv6 strongly recommends PMTUD; a minimal sender can instead stay within the 1,280-byte minimum link MTU.

options.text: The router forwards it anyway and the next router fragments it
options.explanation: A packet larger than the link MTU can't be transmitted on that link at all, and no IPv6 router fragments.

questions.workedExample: The 1,600-byte IPv6 packet exceeds the 1,500-byte outgoing MTU. An IPv6 forwarding router does not fragment it; it discards it and reports Packet Too Big with MTU 1,500, subject to error-generation/rate rules. The source can adjust packetisation or source fragmentation. IP does not itself guarantee retransmission; recovery depends on the transport/application.

lessons.title: SLAAC, prefixes and identifiers
lessons.summary: Plan subnets from a delegated prefix and trace router advertisements, DAD and interface-identifier privacy choices.
lessons.body:
IPv6 hosts can configure their own addresses from information routers advertise. This lesson covers the /64 convention that makes that work, the steps a host follows, and why the host part of an address matters for privacy.

### The /64 convention

A global address is typically split 64/64: a **prefix** (routing) and an **interface identifier** (the host). Ethernet SLAAC uses **/64** prefixes. Other uses include /127 point-to-point router links and /128 host routes, so IPv6 routing is not limited to /64. Delegation sizes vary. How many /64 subnets a delegated prefix holds depends on the bits between its length and 64:

```formula reference
S = 2^(64 − p)
where
S: the number of /64 subnets that fit inside the delegated prefix
p: the delegated prefix length, for example 56 for a /56; at most 64. The 64 − p bits between it and the /64 boundary number the subnets
In words: every bit between the delegated prefix and /64 doubles the number of subnets a site can create. A /56 gives 256 /64 subnets and a /48 gives 65,536; a single /64 gives exactly one, which cannot be split further for SLAAC.
```

This matters for planning: a home or office given only a /64 has one SLAAC-capable subnet, so separate guest, IoT and staff networks need a larger delegation such as a /56.

### SLAAC: configuring without a server

**Stateless address autoconfiguration** (RFC 4862) lets a host configure itself:

1. Form a **link-local** address by combining the link-local prefix with an interface identifier.
2. Run **duplicate address detection** (DAD): probe the tentative address with Neighbor Solicitation. A conflicting Advertisement or another host's DAD Solicitation can reveal a duplicate; absence of a reply is not an absolute uniqueness guarantee.
3. Send a **Router Solicitation** to `ff02::2` (all routers).
4. A **Router Advertisement** (RA) may carry prefix information and flags. A usable autonomous prefix must have its A flag set and suitable length/lifetimes. The RA source becomes a default-router candidate only with a nonzero router lifetime; an RA need not advertise a prefix or a default route.
5. The host can form an address from an eligible prefix and interface identifier, then perform DAD. Working routing, neighbour resolution and other configuration are still needed for external connectivity.

One historical interface-identifier method derives it from the MAC (**modified EUI-64**): split the 48-bit MAC in half, insert `ff:fe` between the halves to make 64 bits, and flip the universal/local (**U/L**) bit, worth 0x02, in the first byte. Flipping that bit turns a first byte of 00 into 02, or 3c into 3e; every other byte is copied unchanged.

So `00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e` becomes `021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e`. The tell-tale `ff:fe` in the middle makes such identifiers easy to spot. Because the MAC travels with the device, the same identifier appears on every network it joins, letting observers track it across home, office and café. Alternatives include opaque, prefix-dependent **stable identifiers** (RFC 7217) and changing **temporary addresses** (RFC 8981). Which method is enabled depends on the system and configuration; stable identifiers stay the same on one network but change when the prefix changes, and are not freshly randomised for every connection.

RA flags say whether to also use **DHCPv6**: M (managed: get addresses from DHCPv6) and O (other: get options such as DNS from DHCPv6). DNS servers can also be sent in the RA itself (RDNSS). Support for DHCPv6 modes varies across client versions. M/O flags do not force a client to implement a mode, and SLAAC prefix processing is controlled separately by the prefix A flag.

## Key takeaways
- Ethernet SLAAC uses /64 prefixes; routing also supports other lengths.
- Router lifetimes, prefix flags and address lifetimes serve different purposes.
- Modified EUI-64 inserts ff:fe and flips the first byte’s U/L bit.
- Stable opaque and temporary identifiers avoid exposing a MAC-derived identifier; DHCPv6 mode support varies.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4862: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4862)
- [RFC 4291: IPv6 Addressing Architecture](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4291)
- [RFC 7217: Stable opaque interface identifiers](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7217)
- [RFC 8981: Temporary addresses](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8981)

questions.prompt: A small office's ISP delegates a single /64. The office wants separate SLAAC-configured Ethernet subnets for staff, guests and IoT devices, each with its own prefix. What is the problem, and what would solve it?

options.text: No problem: split the /64 into three /66 prefixes for SLAAC
options.explanation: Ethernet SLAAC needs a /64 prefix with a 64-bit interface identifier, so the /64 cannot be subdivided into SLAAC-capable subnets.

options.text: A /64 provides exactly one SLAAC subnet; ask for a larger delegation such as a /56, which contains 256 /64 subnets
options.explanation: Correct. Each bit between the delegated length and /64 doubles the subnet count: a /56 has 8 such bits, enough for 256 /64s.

options.text: Use NAT66 so all three networks can share one /64 without any trade-off
options.explanation: The standardised stateless form, NPTv6 (experimental RFC 6296), maps each internal address to exactly one external address, so it cannot squeeze three internal subnets into one external /64. Only a stateful, port-translating NAT66 could, which brings back NAT's state and end-to-end problems. Neither is a trade-off-free fix for an undersized delegation.

options.text: Ask for a /72, which is larger than a /64
options.explanation: A longer prefix is smaller. A /72 is a fraction of a /64, not a bigger block.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ethernet SLAAC forms addresses from a /64 prefix plus a 64-bit interface identifier.
2. So each SLAAC subnet consumes a whole /64, and a /64 cannot be split into smaller SLAAC subnets.
3. Three separate networks need at least three /64s.
4. A /56 leaves 8 bits between /56 and /64, numbering 256 subnets; a /48 leaves 16 bits, numbering 65,536.
5. Direction check: a larger prefix number means a smaller block, so a /72 would not help.

questions.prompt: A laptop's global IPv6 address at home is `2001:db8:1:1:3e22:fbff:fe12:3456`. At a café it is `2001:db8:99:5:3e22:fbff:fe12:3456`. What does the repeated second half indicate, and what reduces the privacy risk?

options.text: Duplicate address detection failed, so the laptop reused its old address
options.explanation: DAD checks for a conflict on the current link; it does not cause the same interface identifier to follow the device between networks.

options.text: Both are link-local addresses, so they are never seen beyond the local network
options.explanation: These start with a global documentation prefix, not fe80::/10, so they are used beyond the link.

options.text: The identifier is a MAC-derived modified EUI-64 (note the ff:fe in the middle), so the device can be recognised on every network; enable RFC 7217 stable opaque identifiers and/or temporary addresses
options.explanation: Correct. A modified EUI-64 identifier comes from the hardware MAC, so it is the same wherever the laptop goes. Stable opaque identifiers change with the prefix, and temporary addresses change over time.

options.text: RFC 7217 stable identifiers always produce the same identifier on every network, which is what you see here
options.explanation: RFC 7217 identifiers are prefix-dependent: they stay stable on one network but differ between networks.

questions.workedExample:
1. The first 64 bits (the prefix) differ between home and café, as expected.
2. The last 64 bits, the interface identifier, are identical and contain `ff:fe` in the middle: the signature of modified EUI-64, built from the MAC address.
3. A stable hardware-derived identifier lets any observer link the laptop's activity across networks.
4. RFC 7217 opaque identifiers are derived per prefix, so they change between networks; RFC 8981 temporary addresses change over time and are used for outgoing connections.
5. The `ff:fe` pattern suggests EUI-64 but cannot prove how an identifier was generated; check the host's configuration.

questions.prompt: A firewall drops all inbound ICMPv6 on a newly configured Ethernet host. Which functions depend on messages this rule blocks? Select all that apply.

options.text: Resolving the default router's link-layer address (Neighbor Discovery)
options.explanation: Correct. Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement are ICMPv6 messages. Without a usable cached/static mapping or other mechanism, rejecting advertisements prevents normal neighbour resolution.

options.text: Learning the prefix and default router via SLAAC
options.explanation: Correct. Prefix information for SLAAC and default-router discovery arrive in Router Advertisements. Address configuration and default-route learning are distinct functions.

options.text: Receiving router MTU feedback for classical path MTU discovery
options.explanation: Correct. Packet Too Big is ICMPv6. Packetisation-layer probing may recover without those messages, so not every large transfer must fail.

options.text: The server's IPv4 traffic
options.explanation: An ICMPv6 rule doesn't touch IPv4 or ICMP for IPv4. The two stacks are filtered separately, which is exactly how IPv6 rules get forgotten.

questions.workedExample: Inbound ICMPv6 includes neighbour advertisements, router advertisements and Packet Too Big messages. Filtering all of it removes those inputs. Static/cached configuration or packetisation-layer probing may mask some failures, but do not make the rule harmless. An ICMPv6-only rule does not directly match IPv4 packets. RFC 4890 discusses filtering by message role.

lessons.title: Dual stack and IPv6 transition
lessons.summary: Explain staggered connection attempts, how NAT64/DNS64 reach IPv4-only servers, and common IPv6 policy pitfalls.
lessons.body:
IPv4 and IPv6 will run side by side for a long time. This lesson covers how clients choose between them and how IPv6-only networks still reach IPv4-only services.

### Dual stack and transition

The two protocols aren't wire-compatible: an IPv6-only host can't talk to an IPv4-only host directly. The migration uses:

- **Dual stack**: hosts and networks run both protocol families.
- **Happy Eyeballs** (RFC 8305): clients resolve and order addresses, then stagger connection attempts across candidates instead of waiting for a failed family's full timeout. The recommended default connection-attempt delay is 250 ms, but implementations can adapt it; DNS timing, address ordering and path RTT affect the result. It is not a universal 250 ms page-load guarantee.
- **NAT64 + DNS64** (RFC 6146/6147): a translator can connect IPv6-only clients to IPv4 servers. DNS64 can synthesise AAAA records using a configured translation prefix; `64:ff9b::/96` is the well-known prefix, not the only option. 464XLAT adds a translator on the client device for IPv4-dependent applications. Reachability and application compatibility still depend on the deployment.
- **Tunnels** (6in4 and others) carry IPv6 over IPv4 links where native IPv6 isn't available.

How a NAT64 connection works, step by step:

1. An IPv6-only phone asks its DNS64 resolver for the AAAA record of an IPv4-only site.
2. Finding no real AAAA record, DNS64 takes the site's A record and synthesises an IPv6 address by placing the 32-bit IPv4 address inside the NAT64 prefix (with the well-known /96 prefix, it fills the last 32 bits).
3. The phone sends ordinary IPv6 packets to that synthesised address. They are routed to the NAT64 translator.
4. The translator extracts the embedded IPv4 address, translates the packet to IPv4 using one of its own shared public IPv4 addresses, and keeps per-connection state so replies can be translated back, much like NAPT.

The IPv4 server sees an ordinary IPv4 client. Applications that skip DNS and use an IPv4 literal address, or open IPv4-only sockets, never get a synthesised address; 464XLAT handles those with a translation layer on the client.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> Current IPv6 adoption percentages, client-platform DHCPv6 support, app-store requirements and consumer NAT timeout surveys are omitted because they need versioned or dated evidence not established here. The linked standards define behaviour, not deployment prevalence.

> [!warning] Common IPv6 pitfalls
> - Review IPv6 firewall policy separately: IPv4-only rules do not establish what the IPv6 policy permits or blocks.
> - Blanket ICMPv6 filtering can break neighbour discovery, router advertisements and MTU feedback. Cached/static configuration or probing may mask some failures; ICMPv6 message types need deliberate treatment.
> - Code that stores IPs in 32-bit integers or splits on `:` for ports (`[2001:db8::1]:443` needs brackets).

## Key takeaways
- Happy Eyeballs staggers candidates; its 250 ms recommendation is not a page-load guarantee.
- DNS64 embeds an IPv4 address in a synthesised IPv6 address; a stateful NAT64 translator turns that traffic into IPv4.
- IPv4 literals bypass DNS64 and need translation on the client device, such as 464XLAT.
- IPv6 requires its own firewall policy and appropriate ICMPv6 treatment.
- IPv6 literals containing ports need bracket-aware parsing.

## Further reading

- [RFC 6146: Stateful NAT64](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6146)
- [RFC 6147: DNS64](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6147)
- [RFC 6052: IPv6 addressing of IPv4/IPv6 translators](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6052)

options.text: The page never loads, because IPv6 is always preferred
options.explanation: That was the problem Happy Eyeballs was designed to solve. Clients no longer wait for IPv6 to time out.

options.text: The page loads after the full TCP connect timeout (tens of seconds) on IPv6, then IPv4
options.explanation: This is pre-Happy-Eyeballs behaviour. Happy Eyeballs starts IPv4 in parallel after a short delay instead of waiting for the IPv6 attempt to fail.

options.text: It starts an IPv4 connection attempt without waiting for the IPv6 attempt to time out
options.explanation: Correct under the stated configuration. IPv4 still needs its own connection and application work; this does not fix total page-load time at 250 ms.

options.text: The browser tunnels IPv6 over IPv4 to reach the site
options.explanation: Browsers don't set up 6in4 tunnels. Happy Eyeballs just races the two address families.

questions.workedExample: The configured timer permits another candidate attempt at about 250 ms while IPv6 is pending. A successful IPv4 connection can then be used. RFC 8305 recommends this default delay but permits adaptive behaviour; DNS timing, address order, immediate errors and implementations can change the sequence.

questions.prompt: An IPv6-only phone on a network with DNS64 and stateful NAT64 opens a web page on a server that has only an IPv4 address. Which description of what happens is correct?

options.text: DNS64 returns a synthesised AAAA record containing the server's IPv4 address inside the NAT64 prefix; the phone sends IPv6 to it, and the translator converts to IPv4 using its own IPv4 address and keeps per-connection state
options.explanation: Correct. The client needs no IPv4 at all for this name-based connection. The translator shares its public IPv4 addresses among clients, much like NAPT.

options.text: The phone quietly obtains an IPv4 address by DHCP and connects natively
options.explanation: The network is IPv6-only, and DNS64/NAT64 exist precisely so the client does not need IPv4 connectivity.

options.text: The translator tunnels the phone's IPv6 packets inside IPv4, so the server must also run IPv6
options.explanation: A tunnel would deliver IPv6 to the server, which only speaks IPv4. NAT64 translates between the protocols instead.

options.text: It works the same way if the app connects to a hard-coded IPv4 literal
options.explanation: An IPv4 literal skips DNS, so no synthesised address is ever produced. A translator on the client device, such as 464XLAT's, is needed for that case.

questions.workedExample:
1. The phone asks for the server's AAAA record.
2. None exists, so DNS64 fetches the A record and embeds that IPv4 address in the configured NAT64 prefix (for the well-known 64:ff9b::/96, the last 32 bits).
3. The phone sends IPv6 packets to the synthesised address; routing brings them to the NAT64 translator.
4. The translator recovers the IPv4 address from the destination, sends IPv4 from one of its own addresses, and records state so replies can be translated back.
5. Because the trick happens in DNS, applications using IPv4 literals miss it; 464XLAT covers them.

lessons.title: Find a route with longest-prefix match
lessons.summary: Separate routing from forwarding and predict which installed route longest-prefix match selects.
lessons.body:
A router does two different jobs, on two very different timescales.

- **Routing** decides *where* each destination should go. It runs protocols (OSPF, BGP), swaps information with neighbours and computes paths. Reaction time depends on failure detection, protocol timers, implementation and topology.
- **Forwarding** takes one packet, looks up its destination, and sends it out of the right interface. It is performed per packet; latency and throughput depend on implementation and workload.

The first is the **control plane**; the second is the **data plane**. Keeping them apart is the central idea of router design. These short lessons examine the data plane: the table, lookup and per-hop work. Later units cover the protocols that fill the table.

## The routing table

A routing table is a list of entries. Each says "packets for this **prefix** go to this **next hop**, out of this **interface**".

| Prefix | Next hop | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| 192.168.1.0/24 | (direct) | eth0 |
| 10.0.0.0/8 | 192.168.1.254 | eth0 |
| 0.0.0.0/0 | 203.0.113.1 | eth1 |

Entries come from three places:

- **Connected routes** are commonly installed when an interface is configured and usable; options can suppress automatic prefix-route installation. Configure `192.168.1.1/24` on eth0 and the router knows 192.168.1.0/24 is directly reachable there.
- **Static routes** are typed in by an operator.
- **Dynamic routes** are learnt from a routing protocol.

The **default route** `0.0.0.0/0` matches every address. It means "if nothing better matches, send it here". A simple home-network example has a connected route and a default route pointing at the home router; VPNs and other configuration can add more.

On Linux:

```
$ ip route
default via 192.168.1.1 dev wlan0
10.8.0.0/24 dev tun0 scope link
192.168.1.0/24 dev wlan0 scope link

$ ip route get 10.8.0.7
10.8.0.7 dev tun0 src 10.8.0.2
```

`ip route get` is the most useful command here: it tells you which route the kernel would actually pick for an address. (Output trimmed for width.)

## Longest-prefix match

With CIDR, prefixes overlap. 10.1.2.9 is inside 0.0.0.0/0, 10.0.0.0/8, 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.1.2.0/24 all at once. Which wins?

The rule is **longest-prefix match** (LPM): of all the entries that contain the destination, use the one with the **longest** prefix, because it's the most specific.

Consider this table:

| Prefix | Next hop |
|---|---|
| 0.0.0.0/0 | isp |
| 10.0.0.0/8 | core |
| 10.1.0.0/16 | dc1 |
| 10.1.2.0/24 | rack7 |

Trace a few destinations:

| Destination | Matches | Winner |
|---|---|---|
| 10.1.2.9 | /0, /8, /16, /24 | rack7 |
| 10.1.3.1 | /0, /8, /16 | dc1 |
| 10.200.0.1 | /0, /8 | core |
| 8.8.8.8 | /0 | isp |

Why "most specific wins"? It lets aggregation and exceptions coexist. A provider announces one big block, and a customer who moved elsewhere announces a smaller piece of it. The smaller, more precise announcement takes priority for its addresses without anyone having to delete the big one.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A mail-sorting rulebook
> A sorting office has rules of different precision: "anything for the UK goes to the national hub", "anything for one postcode area goes to that city's sorting centre", "anything for one district within that area goes to its local delivery office". A letter for that district matches all three, and the clerk follows the most precise one.
>
> **How it maps:** Each rule is a route; the precision of the rule is the prefix length; "anything at all goes to the hub" is the default route 0.0.0.0/0. The order rules were written in does not matter, only their precision.
>
> **Where it stops:** Routers compare binary prefixes of a fixed-length number, not names, and a rule's "precision" is exactly its count of matching bits. And the chosen rule only picks the next hop; the next router repeats the decision with its own table.

> [!warning] More specific always beats "better"
> An eligible /24 installed in the selected forwarding table takes precedence over an installed /16. Rejected routes or unresolved next hops do not participate, and policy can select a different table. Metrics and protocol preferences only break ties between routes for the **same prefix**. This catches people out when a stray static route or a leaked more-specific steals traffic.

### What if nothing matches?

If no entry, not even a default route, contains the destination, the router has nowhere to send the packet. It discards it and normally returns ICMP Destination Unreachable (network unreachable), subject to rate limits and suppression rules. A host with no default route behaves similarly: connections to off-link destinations fail immediately with "network unreachable".

### How fast is the lookup?

The simplest lookup compares the destination with every route and keeps the longest match. That work grows in proportion to the table size, which is fine for a home router's handful of routes but not for a router holding hundreds of thousands. The next lessons cover structures that avoid scanning every entry.

## Key takeaways
- The control plane selects routing state; the data plane forwards packets.
- Connected, static and dynamic routes can populate a table; /0 is the fallback match.
- Among installed eligible prefixes in the selected table, the longest matching IP prefix wins.
- With no matching route at all, the packet is discarded, normally with an ICMP Destination Unreachable.

## Further reading

- [Routing table — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Routing_table)
- [Administrative distance — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_distance)
- [Equal-cost multi-path routing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal-cost_multi-path_routing)
- [RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812)
- [ip-route(8) manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip-route.8.html)

- [Cisco: Administrative distance versus forwarding](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/ip/border-gateway-protocol-bgp/15986-admin-distance.html)
- [Linux LC-trie implementation notes](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/fib_trie.html)
- [RFC 2992: ECMP analysis](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2992.html)
- [Cisco FN63866: TCAM exhaustion](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/field-notices/638/fn63866.html)

questions.prompt:
A router has these routes:

| Prefix | Next hop |
|---|---|
| 0.0.0.0/0 | A |
| 172.16.0.0/12 | B |
| 172.16.4.0/22 | C |
| 172.16.5.0/25 | D |

Where does it send a packet for 172.16.5.9? Assume these are eligible installed routes in the selected forwarding table, with no overriding policy.

options.text: A, because the default route matches everything
options.explanation: The default route does match, but it's the least specific (/0). It only wins when nothing longer matches.

options.text: B, because it was the first specific route in the table
options.explanation: Table order doesn't matter. Longest-prefix match compares prefix lengths, not position.

options.text: C, because 172.16.5.9 is inside 172.16.4.0/22
options.explanation: It is inside the /22 (172.16.4.0 to 172.16.7.255), but a longer match also exists.

options.text: D, because the /25 is the longest prefix that contains it
options.explanation: Correct. 172.16.5.0/25 covers 172.16.5.0 to 172.16.5.127, so .9 is inside it, and /25 is longer than /22, /12 and /0.

questions.prompt: A router's table contains only `10.0.0.0/8`, `10.1.0.0/16` and `10.1.2.0/24`: there is no default route. A packet for 8.8.8.8 arrives. What happens?

options.text: It uses 10.0.0.0/8, the shortest and broadest route
options.explanation: Longest-prefix match only considers entries that contain the destination. 8.8.8.8 is not inside 10.0.0.0/8, so that route is not a candidate.

options.text: It discards the packet and normally sends ICMP Destination Unreachable (network unreachable) back to the source, subject to rate limits
options.explanation: Correct. With no matching entry there is no next hop. RFC 1812 requires a router to discard such a packet and generate a Network Unreachable error, though rate limiting and suppression rules can stop the message being sent.

options.text: It floods the packet out of every interface
options.explanation: IP routers do not flood unicast packets they cannot route; flooding unknown destinations is switch behaviour for unknown MAC addresses.

options.text: It holds the packet until a routing protocol learns a route
options.explanation: Routers forward or drop each packet immediately; they do not queue packets waiting for future routes.

questions.workedExample:
1. List the routes that contain 8.8.8.8: none of the three 10.x prefixes do.
2. There is no 0.0.0.0/0 default to catch everything else.
3. With no matching route there is no next hop, so the packet is discarded.
4. The router normally reports ICMP Destination Unreachable, code 0 (network unreachable), to the source; rate limits can suppress it.
5. On the sender, this often appears as an immediate 'network unreachable' error rather than a slow timeout.

lessons.title: Select routes and program the FIB
lessons.summary: Distinguish same-prefix source preference from packet lookup and explain RIB/FIB responsibilities.
lessons.body:
Distinguish same-prefix source preference from packet lookup and explain RIB/FIB responsibilities.

## When routes tie: distance and metric

Route selection and packet lookup are separate stages. For a Cisco-style destination-based setup:

1. A routing protocol selects candidate paths using its own rules and metrics.
2. For the same exact prefix, the routing table compares eligible candidates from different sources using administrative distance. Lower values are preferred; next-hop reachability also matters.
3. Selected usable routes are programmed for forwarding. A packet lookup then uses **longest-prefix match** among installed prefixes, without comparing administrative distances again.

Metrics from different protocols are not directly interchangeable. Policy routing can choose another table or action before this lookup.

Selected Cisco default administrative distances (configurable and not a universal IP standard):

| Source | Distance |
|---|---|
| Connected | 0 |
| Static | 1 |
| eBGP | 20 |
| OSPF | 110 |
| RIP | 120 |
| iBGP | 200 |

The Linux kernel exposes route priorities/metrics and policy-rule tables, rather than the Cisco source-distance table as a universal kernel mechanism. Routing daemons can apply their own source preferences before installing routes. A lower metric is relevant among otherwise comparable routes, not a replacement for prefix matching or policy.

A common trick uses this: a **floating static** route is a static route given a *high* distance (say 250). It can take over after the preferred route is withdrawn, provided the backup remains eligible and its next hop resolves. Upstream failure need not immediately withdraw a route.

## RIB and FIB

The table described so far is really two:

- The control plane has routing databases (**RIBs**) and protocol-specific state. Which losing candidates are kept in a shared RIB versus a protocol database depends on the implementation.
- The **FIB** (forwarding information base) represents selected forwarding actions, potentially with multiple next hops, recursive resolution and special local/discard entries.

The control plane computes the RIB and pushes changes down to the FIB. Distributed hardware routers can retain programmed forwarding while the control plane is busy or restarting. That does not guarantee continued correct service: failed adjacencies, stale state, shared resources and recovery behaviour still matter.

## Key takeaways
- Administrative distance is a vendor-specific source preference for the same prefix.
- Metrics from different protocols are not interchangeable.
- A floating static route requires the preferred route to become ineligible and the backup to remain usable.
- Retained hardware forwarding state does not guarantee correct service after control-plane failure.

## Further reading

questions.prompt:
A Cisco-style router (default administrative distances) has:

- a static route 10.1.0.0/16 via X
- an OSPF route 10.1.0.0/16 via Y
- an OSPF route 10.1.5.0/24 via Z

Where do packets for 10.1.5.5 and 10.1.9.9 go? Assume next hops are reachable and candidates are otherwise eligible.

options.text: Both go to X, because static routes (distance 1) beat OSPF (110)
options.explanation: Distance is only compared between routes for the *same* prefix. The /24 is a different, more specific prefix, so it wins for 10.1.5.5 whatever its source.

options.text: 10.1.5.5 goes to Z; 10.1.9.9 goes to X
options.explanation: Correct. During route selection the static /16 beats the OSPF /16. Both the winning /16 and the separate /24 are installed. LPM then chooses Z for .5.5 and X for .9.9.

options.text: 10.1.5.5 goes to Z; 10.1.9.9 goes to Y
options.explanation: LPM is right for the first, but for the tied /16s the lower administrative distance wins, and static (1) is lower than OSPF (110).

options.text: Both go to Y, because dynamic routes override static ones
options.explanation: In this stated default Cisco comparison, static distance 1 is preferred to OSPF 110 for the same prefix. That does not mean every configured static route is usable.

questions.workedExample: First select routes for each prefix: static distance 1 beats OSPF 110 for 10.1/16. The separate OSPF 10.1.5/24 is also installed. At packet lookup, 10.1.5.5 matches /24 and uses Z; 10.1.9.9 matches the selected /16 and uses X. Protocol state may retain the losing candidate; exact database placement is implementation-dependent. Administrative distance is not reconsidered for every forwarded packet.

questions.prompt: An engineer adds `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1 250` (a static default with distance 250) on a router that also learns a default route from OSPF (distance 110) via its primary link. What happens? Assume these are the only default candidates and the static next hop remains resolvable.

options.text: The static route is used immediately because static routes always beat dynamic ones
options.explanation: A static route with an eligible distance below 110 can beat this OSPF route; it need not use the default of 1. Here 250 is higher than 110, so OSPF is preferred.

options.text: Traffic is split evenly between both routes by ECMP
options.explanation: ECMP needs routes that tie. Different administrative distances aren't a tie; only the lower one is installed.

options.text: The configuration is rejected because two default routes can't coexist
options.explanation: Multiple configured or learned candidates can coexist. Selection determines which usable forwarding entries are installed.

options.text: The OSPF default is used; the static one takes over only if the OSPF route disappears
options.explanation: Correct. This is a floating static route: its high distance keeps it out of the FIB until the preferred route is withdrawn, giving a simple backup path.

questions.workedExample: For the same default prefix, OSPF distance 110 beats static 250. If OSPF withdraws its route and the static remains resolvable, the static can be installed. When eligible OSPF returns it is preferred again. An upstream failure does not necessarily cause immediate withdrawal; detection and tracking matter.

lessons.title: Follow a packet across Ethernet hops
lessons.summary: Trace TTL, checksum and link-address changes, and choose which next-hop address ARP resolves.
lessons.body:
Trace TTL, checksum and link-address changes, and choose which next-hop address ARP resolves.

## What happens at each hop

For an ordinary forwarded IPv4 unicast packet on Ethernet, with no NAT, tunnel, options processing or fragmentation, the logical work includes (the hardware pipeline order can differ):

1. Checks the IPv4 header checksum (and drops on failure).
2. Decrements **TTL**. If it expires, drops the packet and normally reports ICMP Time Exceeded, subject to suppression/rate rules.
3. Updates the header checksum, possibly incrementally.
4. Looks up the destination with LPM to get next hop and interface.
5. Resolves the Ethernet next-hop MAC through ARP, using a valid cached mapping when available. IPv6 instead uses Neighbor Discovery and has no base-header checksum.
6. Builds a new link-layer frame and sends it.

In this Ethernet unicast example, IP source/destination remain unchanged while each routed link uses its next-hop MAC addressing. Other link technologies need not use MAC addresses, and tunnels, NAT and special routing mechanisms need separate treatment.

```
Host A        Router R1       Host B
10.0.0.5      10.0.0.1 |      10.9.0.7
mac aa        mac r1a  | r1b  mac bb

Frame 1 (A to R1)
  src mac aa   dst mac r1a
  src ip 10.0.0.5 dst ip 10.9.0.7

Frame 2 (R1 to B)
  src mac r1b  dst mac bb
  src ip 10.0.0.5 dst ip 10.9.0.7
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A parcel and its courier stickers
> A parcel's address label names the final recipient and never changes. For each leg of the journey, the depot sticks a fresh routing sticker on top saying only "to the next depot" and peels off the previous one.
>
> **How it maps:** The address label is the IP header with its source and destination; the per-leg sticker is the Ethernet frame with the next hop's MAC address. Each router (depot) reads the label, picks the next leg from its table, and writes a new sticker.
>
> **Where it stops:** A router also changes the label slightly at every hop, decrementing TTL and updating the header checksum. NAT and tunnels change much more, and links that are not Ethernet may use no MAC addresses at all.

A host does the same LPM decision. If the selected route marks the destination as on-link on Ethernet, it ARPs for the destination itself. For a route via a gateway, it resolves that route's next hop. That may be a more-specific gateway route rather than the default; no matching route is also possible.

## Key takeaways
- Ordinary forwarding decrements TTL and updates the IPv4 header checksum.
- With the stated assumptions, IP endpoints remain unchanged across the router.
- The next Ethernet frame targets the selected next hop, which may be the destination or a gateway.
- The diagram excludes NAT, tunnelling and fragmentation.

## Further reading
- [Longest prefix match — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longest_prefix_match)
- [Routing table — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Routing_table)
- [Administrative distance — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_distance)
- [Equal-cost multi-path routing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal-cost_multi-path_routing)
- [RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812)
- [ip-route(8) manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip-route.8.html)

- [Cisco: Administrative distance versus forwarding](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/ip/border-gateway-protocol-bgp/15986-admin-distance.html)
- [Linux LC-trie implementation notes](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/fib_trie.html)
- [RFC 2992: ECMP analysis](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2992.html)
- [Cisco FN63866: TCAM exhaustion](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/field-notices/638/fn63866.html)

questions.prompt: A packet from host A (10.0.0.5) to host B (10.9.0.7) crosses one router, R1. Without NAT, what is in the frame on the link between A and R1? Assume ordinary Ethernet unicast forwarding without tunnelling, source routing or rewriting.

options.text: Source IP 10.0.0.5, destination IP 10.9.0.7, destination MAC of R1
options.explanation: Correct. IP addresses are end to end, so the destination IP is B. But B isn't on A's link, so the frame is addressed to the next hop's MAC: R1's.

options.text: Source IP 10.0.0.5, destination IP of R1, destination MAC of R1
options.explanation: In this case the gateway IP selects the Ethernet next hop; it does not replace B as the packet destination.

options.text: Source IP 10.0.0.5, destination IP 10.9.0.7, destination MAC of B
options.explanation: The selected next hop is R1, so A resolves R1's local MAC. B is beyond the routed link.

options.text: Source IP of R1, destination IP 10.9.0.7, destination MAC of B
options.explanation: R1 doesn't rewrite source IPs unless it's doing NAT, and this frame hasn't even reached R1 yet.

questions.workedExample:
1. A checks its table: 10.9.0.7 isn't in its connected subnet, and its selected route points via R1.
2. A ARPs for R1's IP to get R1's MAC.
3. A builds the frame: dst MAC = R1, src MAC = A.
4. Inside it, the IP packet keeps src 10.0.0.5, dst 10.9.0.7.
5. R1 will strip the frame, decrement TTL and build a new frame to B with B's MAC. The IPs stay the same throughout.

questions.prompt: A laptop's routing table holds only `192.168.1.0/24 dev wlan0` and `default via 192.168.1.1`. It sends a packet to 8.8.8.8 and its ARP cache is empty. Which IP address does it send an ARP request for?

options.explanation: The selected route names 192.168.1.1 as next hop. Proxy ARP can answer for nonlocal IPs in other configurations, but it does not change this lookup.
That's the subnet's broadcast address. ARP requests are *sent* to the broadcast MAC, but they ask about a specific IP.
Correct. Only the default route matches 8.8.8.8, and its next hop is 192.168.1.1. The laptop needs that router's MAC to build the frame.

options.text: None; the default route means it sends the frame to the broadcast MAC
options.explanation: Unicast IP traffic is never broadcast at layer 2 just because it's off-link. The host resolves the gateway's MAC and unicasts to it.

questions.workedExample:
1. LPM for 8.8.8.8: the /24 doesn't contain it; the /0 does.
2. The default route's next hop is **192.168.1.1**.
3. To deliver a frame to that next hop, the laptop needs its MAC, so it broadcasts "who has 192.168.1.1?".
4. The router replies, the laptop caches the MAC and sends the packet (still addressed to 8.8.8.8 at the IP layer).

questions.prompt: An ordinary IPv4 router forwards a unicast TCP packet between Ethernet links, without NAT, tunnels, fragmentation, options processing or other rewriting. Which actions are required? Select all that apply.

options.text: Decrement the TTL
options.explanation: Correct. Forwarding decrements TTL by at least one; expiry prevents forwarding and normally prompts an ICMP error subject to suppression/rate rules.

options.text: Update the IPv4 header checksum, possibly incrementally
options.explanation: Correct. The header checksum must remain consistent with the TTL change.

options.text: Rewrite the destination IP to the next hop's address
options.explanation: The destination IP stays as the final host's address all the way. The next hop's address is used only to find its MAC.

options.text: Build a new frame with the next hop's MAC as destination
options.explanation: Correct. Link-layer addressing is per hop, so each router writes a fresh frame for the outgoing link.

options.text: Recompute the TCP checksum
options.explanation: TCP's checksum covers the TCP segment plus a pseudo-header of IPs, protocol and length. None of those change at a plain router, so it's untouched. (NAT does have to fix it.)

questions.workedExample: Under these explicit assumptions, forwarding changes TTL and its IPv4 header checksum and constructs an outgoing Ethernet frame for the selected next hop. IP source/destination and TCP bytes remain unchanged, and TTL is not part of the TCP pseudo-header, so the TCP checksum does not need updating. Other router functions can change additional fields outside this scenario.

lessons.title: Accelerate lookup with tries and TCAM
lessons.summary: Compare bitwise trie lookup with a priority-TCAM model and recognise platform capacity limits.
lessons.body:
A backbone router may hold hundreds of thousands of routes and must look one up for every packet. Comparing the destination with every route would be far too slow, so routers use structures whose lookup cost does not grow with the table.

## Fast lookup structures

### Binary tries

Store prefixes in a binary tree keyed by address bits. Walk down from the root following the destination's bits, remembering the last node that held a route. When you can't go further, the last route seen is the longest matching IP prefix.

```
root (0/0: isp)
  | next 8 bits 00001010
node 10/8: core
  | next 8 bits 00000001
node 10.1/16: dc1
  | next 8 bits 00000010
node 10.1.2/24: rack7
```

Each step down the tree consumes one bit of the destination address, so a lookup can never take more steps than the address has bits: at most 32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6, however many routes the table holds. Growing the table from a thousand routes to a million makes a linear scan a thousand times slower but leaves this bound unchanged. In Big-O notation, where W is the address width in bits, the lookup is O(W).

**Patricia** (path-compressed) tries skip chains of single-child nodes, and **multibit** tries consume 4, 8 or more bits per step to cut memory accesses. Linux's IPv4 FIB uses an LC-trie (level- and path-compressed).

### TCAM

Some forwarding hardware uses **TCAM** (ternary content-addressable memory). Each entry stores bits as 0, 1 or "don't care", so `10.1.0.0/16` becomes 16 fixed bits and 16 wildcards. In a simplified priority-TCAM model, entries are compared in parallel and a priority encoder selects a match. Ordering longer prefixes before shorter ones implements LPM in that model. Real designs can combine banks, stages, tries and separate priority logic.

| Structure | Principal trade-off |
|---|---|
| Trie | Follows address bits through memory; compression and layout influence accesses and capacity |
| Priority TCAM | Parallel masked matching with explicit priority; resource cost and lookup timing depend on implementation |

Cisco's 2014 field notice FN63866 documents FIB TCAM exhaustion on specified Catalyst 6500/7600 configurations, including software switching of some entries and possible elevated CPU usage or instability. This is a platform-specific capacity example, not evidence that every router behaves the same when full.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> Universal one-cycle lookup claims, nanosecond forwarding promises and a current global prefix count are omitted because no matching hardware specification or dated measurement is established here.

## Key takeaways
- A binary trie follows at most one edge per address bit and remembers the last route.
- Compression reduces memory accesses without changing longest-prefix semantics.
- A first-match priority TCAM needs longer prefixes before shorter ones.
- The 2014 Cisco capacity incident describes specific platforms and configurations.

## Further reading
