- [Routing table — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Routing_table)
- [Administrative distance — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_distance)
- [Equal-cost multi-path routing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal-cost_multi-path_routing)
- [RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812)
- [ip-route(8) manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip-route.8.html)

- [Cisco: Administrative distance versus forwarding](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/ip/border-gateway-protocol-bgp/15986-admin-distance.html)
- [Linux LC-trie implementation notes](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/fib_trie.html)
- [RFC 2992: ECMP analysis](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2992.html)
- [Cisco FN63866: TCAM exhaustion](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/field-notices/638/fn63866.html)

questions.prompt: A router's IPv4 forwarding table, stored as a plain binary trie, grows from 1,000 routes to 1,000,000. What happens to the worst-case number of steps for one lookup?

options.text: It grows about a thousand-fold, in proportion to the number of routes
options.explanation: That describes a linear scan that compares every route. A trie follows the destination's bits instead of visiting every route.

options.text: It grows a little, like the depth of a balanced search tree over the routes
options.explanation: A balanced tree's depth grows with the logarithm of the number of keys. A trie's depth is set by the key length, not the number of keys.

options.text: It stays bounded by 32, one step per address bit, because the walk follows the destination's bits
options.explanation: Correct. More routes add nodes and memory, but a lookup still takes at most one step per bit of a 32-bit address. Multibit tries cut the step count further by consuming several bits at once.

options.text: It drops to one step, because tries use hashing
options.explanation: A plain binary trie does not hash; it walks bit by bit. One-step claims belong to specific hardware designs, not to tries in general.

questions.workedExample:
1. In a binary trie, each step down consumes one bit of the destination address.
2. An IPv4 address has 32 bits, so no walk can be longer than 32 steps (128 for IPv6).
3. Adding routes adds nodes and memory but cannot make the address longer.
4. A linear scan, by contrast, makes one comparison per route, so it slows a thousand-fold.
5. Real lookup time also depends on memory layout, caching and compression; the bound is on abstract steps, not nanoseconds.

questions.prompt: A software bug loads a router's TCAM with entries sorted **shortest prefix first**, including 0.0.0.0/0. The TCAM returns the first matching entry. What happens to traffic?

options.text: Nothing changes; TCAM always finds the longest matching IP prefix regardless of order
options.explanation: The question specifies a first-match priority TCAM. This model needs an ordering/priority scheme that implements LPM; not every hardware design has identical ordering semantics.

options.text: Everything goes to the default route, because 0.0.0.0/0 is first and matches every address
options.explanation: Correct. The /0 entry is all wildcards, so it matches every lookup. With it at the top, every more specific route is hidden behind it.

options.text: Lookups slow down to a linear scan
options.explanation: Changing entry order changes this priority model's chosen match; it does not turn the specified parallel matching operation into a sequential scan.

options.text: Packets with no specific route are dropped
options.explanation: It's the reverse: the default matches first, so even destinations with specific routes go to the default next hop.

questions.workedExample:
1. TCAM entry for 0.0.0.0/0: 32 "don't care" bits. It matches anything.
2. Every entry is compared in parallel; the priority encoder picks the lowest-index match.
3. With shortest first, index 0 is the /0. It always matches, so it always wins.
4. Result: every packet goes to the default next hop.
5. Correct ordering puts /32s first and /0 last, so the first match is the longest.

questions.prompt: Which statements about hardware forwarding capacity and Cisco's documented 2014 TCAM-exhaustion issue are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Some documented Catalyst 6500/7600 configurations had a finite default FIB TCAM allocation and could enter an exception state when exceeded
options.explanation: Correct. Cisco FN63866 documents the affected configurations and default 512k allocation; this is not a universal limit for all routers.

options.text: Cisco reported that some entries could be software switched, with possible elevated CPU usage and connectivity impact
options.explanation: Correct for the documented exception condition. This does not prove every overflowing router uses the same fallback.

options.text: TCAMs are used because they are cheap and low-power compared with DRAM
options.explanation: TCAM provides parallel masked matching, but its cost, power and timing depend on the design. It is not universally cheap, low-power or a one-cycle complete forwarding pipeline.

options.text: Correct aggregation can reduce the prefix entries a receiving router must represent
options.explanation: Correct. Actual FIB savings depend on accepted routes, remaining more-specifics, address families and hardware encoding; every advertisement need not become one entry everywhere.

questions.workedExample: Cisco's field notice documents particular finite TCAM allocations and exception behaviour, including software switching of some entries. Routing visibility and hardware allocation are deployment-specific. Proper aggregation can reduce represented prefixes, but advertised aggregates must preserve intended reachability and cannot be treated as an unconditional fix for every capacity problem.

lessons.title: ECMP, asymmetry and route failures
lessons.summary: Explain flow hashing, path churn and legitimate asymmetric routing, then organise failure checks.
lessons.body:
Real networks often have several equally good paths, and replies need not follow the same path as requests. Both facts are normal, and both surprise anyone who assumes one fixed path.

## Multiple paths: ECMP

If the routing implementation and policy select multiple eligible paths for the same prefix, the router can install a next-hop group: **equal-cost multi-path** (ECMP). Data centres rely on it to spread traffic over many links.

A common ECMP policy hashes flow-identifying fields, often the IP/port/protocol 5-tuple. Keeping a stable flow on a stable path reduces reordering, which can trigger spurious loss recovery in TCP. Hash inputs vary, and per-packet or flowlet policies also exist. Path changes and fragmentation can disrupt flow affinity; neither ECMP nor TCP treats every reordered packet as lost.

The trade-offs:

- A few huge flows ("elephants") can land on the same link while others sit idle.
- Reusing correlated hashes with similarly ordered next-hop groups can make downstream routers repeat the same path choices (**hash polarisation**). Different hash seeds can reduce correlated choices, without guaranteeing perfect balance.
- When a path is added or removed, naive modulo hashing remaps many flows. **Resilient hashing** limits the churn.

Naive modulo hashing picks a next hop by hashing the flow and taking the remainder after dividing by the number of paths:

```formula reference
i = H(f) mod k
where
i: the index of the chosen next hop, from 0 to k − 1
H(f): a hash function applied to f, giving a large whole number that looks random but is always the same for the same input
f: the flow's identifying fields, such as the 5-tuple of addresses, ports and protocol
mod: modulo: the remainder after whole-number division, so 14 mod 4 = 2 and 14 mod 3 = 2
k: the number of next hops in the equal-cost group
In words: hash the flow and take the remainder after dividing by the number of paths. The same flow always lands on the same path while the number of paths stays the same; change that number and most flows are reassigned.
```

Changing the path count can remap many flows. For the specific change from four paths to three, assume roughly uniform hashes, remove the last-indexed path, and keep the surviving path indices unchanged. A flow keeps its path only when its hash gives the same remainder in both groups: one quarter of possible residues over the shared twelve-value cycle. About three quarters of flows therefore move, although only the quarter on the removed path needed a new path. Different group reordering or nonuniform traffic changes the observed result.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Checkout lanes by surname
> A shop with four tills sends each family to a till chosen from the first letter of their surname, so a family always queues together and its shopping is never split across tills. When one till closes, the manager redraws the letter ranges across the remaining three.
>
> **How it maps:** Each family is a flow, the surname rule is the hash, and the tills are the equal-cost next hops. Keeping a family at one till is flow affinity, which reduces the chance of packets of one connection arriving out of order. Redrawing the ranges moves many families who were not at the closed till: the churn of naive modulo hashing.
>
> **Where it stops:** A shop can see one family with a huge trolley and move it; a simple hash cannot tell an elephant flow from a small one. Resilient hashing keeps the surviving assignments fixed, which the redrawn-letters picture does not capture.

## Asymmetric routing

With ordinary destination-based forwarding, each router makes its own decision; policy routing can consider other fields. Nothing forces the reply to come back the same way, and on the Internet it often doesn't. That's normal, but it breaks things that assume symmetry:

- **Stateful firewalls** may reject traffic when the necessary connection state is absent. Asymmetric-routing support or state shared between firewalls can change the outcome.
- **Strict reverse path filtering** checks whether the ingress interface is a best route back towards the source. It can reject legitimate asymmetric traffic. Loose modes instead check source reachability without requiring the same interface; Linux policy and configuration affect the lookup. Choose a mode appropriate to the routing design.

### Source-specific reply routing

A multihomed Linux server can need different defaults for different local source addresses. A destination outside both connected subnets would otherwise follow the selected main-table default. If replies sourced from `192.168.50.5` must use the gateway on eth1, configure a separate table containing eth1’s connected prefix and its reachable gateway default, then add a suitably prioritised source rule for that address. The connected route lets that table resolve its gateway. Check the resulting lookup with `ip route get` including the source address; an earlier rule or policy can change the result. Packet captures must establish where replies actually leave, and firewall/reverse-path checks remain separate.

## Pitfalls

- **Routing loops**: two routers each pointing at the other for a prefix. Packets bounce until TTL expires; traceroute may show repeated responders, but filtering, rate limits and varying paths can obscure the pattern.
- **Black holes**: a route exists, but the next hop is dead or drops traffic. Operators also create them deliberately with **null routes** to discard attack traffic.
- **Missing return route**: you add a route to a new subnet, but the far side has no route back. Pings go out and nothing returns.

## Key takeaways
- Flow hashing helps preserve packet order on stable paths but does not guarantee equal utilisation.
- Changing a naive modulo path count can move flows that did not use the removed path.
- Reply routes can differ; stateful filters and reverse-path checks must fit the design.
- A present route does not prove a working next hop or network reply path.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: A switch uses stable per-flow 5-tuple hashing over four equal-cost uplinks. What is a principal reason to choose this instead of per-packet round-robin across paths with different delays?

options.text: Hashing spreads load more evenly than round-robin
options.explanation: Round-robin balances packet counts across the four links, but varying packet sizes and link conditions mean that is not necessarily balanced byte load or utilisation. Flow hashing can also be imbalanced when large flows collide.

options.text: Round-robin isn't allowed by the IP specification
options.explanation: Nothing in IP forbids it. It's avoided for a transport-layer reason.

options.text: It reduces cross-path reordering that can trigger spurious transport loss recovery
options.explanation: Correct. Path affinity reduces one source of reordering; TCP can tolerate some reordering, and the exact recovery response depends on the algorithm.

options.text: Hashing lets the switch skip the routing table lookup
options.explanation: The lookup still happens; it returns a set of next hops, and the hash picks one of them.

questions.workedExample: Packets sent over different paths can arrive out of order because delays differ. Stable flow hashing tends to keep a flow on one next hop while the path set and hash inputs remain stable, reducing that cause of reordering. It does not guarantee order during path changes, and elephant flows can still produce imbalance. Per-packet ECMP is possible; this is a design trade-off, not an IP prohibition.

questions.prompt: A Linux server has eth0 (10.0.0.5/24, default via 10.0.0.1) and eth1 (192.168.50.5/24, connected route only). A SYN from 192.168.60.20 to 192.168.50.5 arrives via eth1. Captures confirm it is accepted and the SYN-ACK leaves eth0, but the required network reply path is via 192.168.50.1. No overriding policy applies. Which change can direct replies from 192.168.50.5 through eth1?

options.text: Install a source-specific routing table with the eth1 connected route and gateway default, plus an appropriately prioritised rule for source 192.168.50.5
options.explanation: Correct. The current default selects eth0. A complete source-specific table can select eth1 for replies with this source; a destination-specific route is another option for a narrower requirement.

options.text: ARP fails on eth1; add a static ARP entry for the client
options.explanation: The client isn't on eth1's link, so the server never ARPs for it. The issue is which route the reply uses.

options.text: The server's TTL is too low; raise net.ipv4.ip_default_ttl
options.explanation: The captures establish which interface the reply leaves by. Raising TTL does not select the desired next hop.

options.text: Linux can't reply from a different interface's address; bind the service to 10.0.0.5
options.explanation: Linux will happily send a packet with source 192.168.50.5 out of eth0. That's precisely the problem, not a limitation.

questions.workedExample:
The destination 192.168.60.20 matches neither connected subnet, so the main default selects eth0. For the specified source-specific requirement, an illustrative configuration is:

```sh
ip route add 192.168.50.0/24 \
  dev eth1 scope link table 100
ip route add default \
  via 192.168.50.1 dev eth1 table 100
ip rule add priority 1000 \
  from 192.168.50.5/32 table 100
```

Assume table 100 and priority 1000 are unused and no earlier rule overrides the lookup. Validate the result with `ip route get` including the source. The table needs gateway reachability, not just a bare default. Firewall and reverse-path settings are separate checks; captures, not missing replies alone, established this route choice.

lessons.title: Learn routes with distance vectors
lessons.summary: Explain the Bellman–Ford neighbour rule and interpret the RIP metric and update rules.
lessons.body:
The forwarding lessons assumed the routing table was already full. In a network of three routers you could type the routes in by hand. In a network of three hundred, with links failing and being added, you need routers to work it out themselves.

That's what **routing protocols** do. **Interior gateway protocols** (IGPs) operate within a routing domain. An **autonomous system** is an administratively coordinated network or group of networks with a routing policy; one organisation can operate multiple ASes. BGP exchanges inter-AS routes and is also used internally.

There are two classic designs:

- **Distance vector**: each router tells its neighbours "here's how far I am from everything". Nobody sees the whole map. RIP is the textbook example.
- **Link state**: routers propagate link information within the relevant scope, such as an OSPF area. Each router builds that scope's map and computes shortest paths itself. OSPF and IS-IS work this way.

## Distance vector and RIP

### The idea

Each router keeps a table of `destination -> (distance, next hop)`. Periodically it sends that table to its neighbours. When it hears a neighbour's table, it applies the **Bellman–Ford** rule:

```formula essential
D(x, d) = min_n (c(x, n) + D(n, d))
where
D(x, d): router x's best known distance (total routing cost) to destination d; for a neighbour n, D(n, d) is the distance n advertised
x: the router doing the calculation
d: the destination network
n: one of x's neighbours; the rule tries every neighbour in turn
c(x, n): the cost of the link from x to neighbour n (normally 1 per network in RIP; larger configured costs are permitted)
min_n: the minimum over all neighbours n: the smallest of the values computed for each neighbour
In words: my best distance to a destination is the cheapest "hop to a neighbour, then their distance", and the neighbour that gives it becomes my next hop.
```

For example, router X hears from neighbour Y (routing link cost 2), which advertises network N at distance 7, and from neighbour Z (routing link cost 5), which advertises N at 3. Via Y the total is 2 + 7 = 9; via Z it is 5 + 3 = 8. X installs N at distance 8 with Z as next hop, even though the link to Y is cheaper: what matters is the whole journey, not the first step.

Routers only ever know what their neighbours told them. It's routing by rumour.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Village signposts
> Imagine each village crossroads has signposts that are repainted from what neighbouring villages say: "the castle is 7 miles via Ashby" or "3 miles via Bramley". The local painter adds the distance to that neighbour and keeps whichever sign gives the shortest total. Nobody holds a full map.
>
> **How it maps:** Each crossroads is a router, the signposts are its routing table (distance and next hop per destination), and the neighbours' reports are distance-vector updates. The painter's rule is the Bellman–Ford update.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real signposts are rarely wrong for long, but a router keeps believing a neighbour's claim until updates or timers correct it. If a bridge collapses, two villages can each point at the other, which is the count-to-infinity problem in the next lesson.

### RIP specifics

The **Routing Information Protocol** provides a compact distance-vector example:

| Property | RIP |
|---|---|
| Metric | Additive integer cost, normally hop count |
| Infinity | 16 (max usable 15) |
| Updates | Periodic eligible-route updates around 30 s, plus triggered updates |
| Transport | UDP port 520 |
| Route timeout | 180 s without refresh |

**RIPv1** (1988) was classful: it didn't send subnet masks and broadcast its updates. **RIPv2** (RFC 2453) carries masks (so CIDR works), uses multicast 224.0.0.9 and supports authentication. **RIPng** is the IPv6 version.

With cost 1 per link, RIP reduces to hop count: two 10 Gbit/s links cost more than one 1 Mbit/s link. RFC 2453 also permits configured higher network costs; RIP does not automatically measure bandwidth. The maximum usable advertised route metric is 15, which is deliberate, for reasons the next section explains.

## Key takeaways
- An IGP operates within a routing domain; distance vector and link state exchange different information.
- Add the local routing link cost to each neighbour’s advertised distance and choose the minimum.
- RIP uses additive costs, normally hop count, with 16 meaning unreachable.
- RIPv2 carries masks and uses UDP port 520; configured costs need not measure bandwidth.

## Further reading
- [RFC 2328: OSPF Version 2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2328)
- [RFC 2453: RIP Version 2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2453)
- [Open Shortest Path First — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Shortest_Path_First)
- [Distance-vector routing protocol — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance-vector_routing_protocol)
- [Link-state routing protocol — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Link-state_routing_protocol)
- [RFC 7938: Use of BGP for Routing in Large-Scale Data Centers](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7938)

- [RFC 5838: OSPFv3 address families](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5838.html)
- [Cisco OSPF FAQ: costs and operational details](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/ip/open-shortest-path-first-ospf/9237-9.html)

questions.prompt: A RIP router receives an update listing a route with metric 16. What does it mean?

options.text: The destination is 16 hops away, the furthest RIP allows
options.explanation: The furthest *usable* distance is 15. 16 is reserved as infinity.

options.text: The route goes over a 16 Mbit/s link
options.explanation: The metric is an additive routing cost, normally hop count when each network costs 1; it is not a measured bandwidth in Mbit/s.

options.text: The route is the 16th entry in the table
options.explanation: Metrics are distances, not positions.

options.text: The destination is unreachable
options.explanation: Correct. Metric 16 marks the route unreachable for forwarding. It may remain temporarily, during RIP's garbage-collection timer, for unreachable advertisements, rather than disappearing immediately.

questions.workedExample:
1. RIP normally uses cost 1 per network, giving hop count; larger configured costs are permitted.
2. Valid distances are 1 to 15.
3. A metric of **16 means infinity: unreachable.**
4. That small infinity bounds how long count to infinity can run, at the cost of limiting usable routes to metric 15 (at most 15 network hops with cost one).

questions.prompt: A distance-vector router X has two neighbours: Y (routing link cost 2) and Z (routing link cost 5). Y advertises destination D at distance 7; Z advertises D at distance 3. What does X install for D?

options.text: Distance 3 via Z
options.explanation: That's Z's distance. X must add the cost of reaching Z (5).

options.text: Distance 9 via Y
options.explanation: 2 + 7 = 9 is X's cost via Y, but via Z is cheaper.

options.text: Distance 8 via Z
options.explanation: Correct. Bellman–Ford takes the cheaper total: 2 + 7 = 9 via Y or 5 + 3 = 8 via Z, so 8 through Z.

options.text: Distance 7 via Y, because Y has the cheaper link
options.explanation: Choosing the cheapest first link ignores what lies beyond it. Distance vector minimises the total.

questions.workedExample:
Apply the distance-vector rule: for each neighbour, add the cost of reaching that neighbour to the distance it advertises, then keep the smallest total.

| Via | Link | Advertised | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Y | 2 | 7 | 9 |
| Z | 5 | 3 | **8** |

Install **8 via Z**. The cheaper first link (to Y) does not decide the choice; the whole journey does. X can then advertise its selected distance according to the protocol's update and split horizon policy.

lessons.title: Trace and limit count to infinity
lessons.summary: Follow a failed route through a distance-vector loop and assess the limits of split horizon and poisoning.
lessons.body:
Follow a failed route through a distance-vector loop and assess the limits of split horizon and poisoning.

### Count to infinity

Distance vector has a famous failure. Take three routers in a line, with network N attached to C. The numbers beneath the routers are their initial hop-count costs to N:

```
 N --- C ------ B ------ A
      1        2        3
```

B reaches N via C at 2 hops, A via B at 3. Now the **B–C link fails**.

Assume plain distance vector without split horizon, poison reverse or an effective hold-down, and that A has not yet learned the failure. B has lost its route. But A's next periodic update says "I can reach N in 3". B doesn't know that A's path *goes through B*, so it believes it:

| Step | B's distance | A's distance |
|---|---|---|
| Before | 2 via C | 3 via B |
| B hears A | 4 via A | 3 via B |
| A hears B | 4 via A | 5 via B |
| B hears A | 6 via A | 5 via B |
| ... | ... | ... |
| End | 16 | 16 |

The two routers bounce the route between them, adding one each time, until it hits 16 and is declared unreachable. Meanwhile packets for N loop between A and B until their TTL runs out. With 30-second updates this can take minutes. That's why RIP's infinity is so small: a larger one would make the count take longer still.

### The fixes

- **Split horizon**: never advertise a route back out of the interface you learnt it from. A learnt N from B, so A doesn't tell B about N. That alone fixes the example above.
- **Poison reverse**: stronger version: *do* advertise it back, but with metric 16 ("don't route via me").
- **Triggered updates**: send changes without waiting for the next periodic update, with a small randomised rate-limiting delay to prevent storms.
- **Hold-down**: some implementations temporarily restrict acceptance of alternatives after failure. Exact rules vary; this is not a universal RIP requirement and can delay valid recovery.

None of these is complete. Simple split horizon prevents the immediate reverse advertisement in this example, but an existing two-router loop may need to time out; poison reverse explicitly advertises infinity to break it. Neither mechanism prevents every loop through three or more routers. Other distance-vector protocols use additional loop-avoidance algorithms; this limitation of basic RIP is not a proof that all distance-vector designs behave identically.

## Key takeaways
- Stale neighbour information can make routers repeatedly increase a false distance.
- Split horizon suppresses reverse advertisements; poison reverse advertises infinity back.
- Triggered updates and implementation-specific hold-downs change recovery behaviour.
- Two-router fixes do not eliminate all longer loops.

## Further reading

- [RFC 2453: RIP Version 2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2453)

questions.prompt: Routers in a line, `N -- C -- B -- A`, run RIP **without** split horizon. B reaches N at 2 via C; A at 3 via B. The B–C link fails. A's next update says "N: 3". What does B do? Assume no hold-down or alternative route, and A's stale update arrives before it processes any failure information.

options.text: Ignores it, because A is further from N than B used to be
options.explanation: Plain distance vector accepts any route better than what it has. B has nothing now, so 3 + 1 looks like an improvement.

options.text: Installs N at 3 via A
options.explanation: B must add its routing link cost to A (1 hop). A's 3 becomes B's 4.

options.text: Marks N unreachable and tells A immediately
options.explanation: That's what triggered updates plus poisoning would aim for, but in this scenario A's update arrives first and B believes it.

options.text: Installs N at 4 via A, creating a loop between A and B
options.explanation: Correct. B can't know A's route goes through B. Packets for N now bounce A to B to A, and the two routers count up by 2 per exchange until 16.

questions.workedExample:
1. B loses its route via C.
2. A advertises N at 3 (its route via B, but B can't tell).
3. B computes 1 + 3 = **4 via A** and installs it.
4. A's route is via B, so A updates to 4 + 1 = 5; then B to 6, and so on.
5. At 16 both declare N unreachable. Until then packets for N loop until TTL expiry.

Split horizon would stop step 2: A wouldn't advertise N to B, the neighbour it learnt it from.

questions.prompt: Which of these are mechanisms distance-vector protocols use to reduce count-to-infinity problems? Select all that apply.

options.text: Split horizon
options.explanation: Correct. Suppress reverse advertisements on the incoming interface. This prevents the lesson's two-router feedback example; an existing two-router loop can still require timeout with simple split horizon.

options.text: Poison reverse
options.explanation: Correct. Advertise the route back to where you learnt it with metric infinity, explicitly telling the neighbour not to use you.

options.text: Raising infinity from 16 to 255 for larger networks
options.explanation: A bigger infinity makes counting to it take *longer*. RIP's tiny infinity is a deliberate trade-off.

options.text: Triggered updates
options.explanation: Correct. Triggered updates do not wait for the next periodic update; small randomised delays rate-limit repeated triggers.

options.text: Implementation-specific hold-down policies
options.explanation: Correct as a possible mitigation. Acceptance rules differ and can delay valid alternatives; RFC 2453 does not prescribe one universal hold-down algorithm.

questions.workedExample:
Count to infinity happens because stale good news ("I can reach N") keeps circulating after a failure.

- Split horizon and poison reverse stop the news going back where it came from.
- Triggered updates spread the bad news faster.
- Implementation-specific hold-down can restrict stale alternatives after a failure; its rules may also delay valid recovery.
- A bigger infinity only lengthens the count. That's the odd one out.

questions.prompt: A RIP network uses split horizon on every router. In which situation can count to infinity still happen?

options.text: Never; split horizon eliminates count to infinity
options.explanation: Split horizon does not prevent every loop through three or more routers. Simple split horizon also need not immediately clear an already existing two-router loop.

options.text: Only when links have different bandwidths
options.explanation: RIP ignores bandwidth. The problem is about topology, not link speed.

options.text: When the failure is inside a loop of three or more routers, so a stale route can travel round the ring and come back via a different neighbour
options.explanation: Correct. Split horizon stops a route going back the way it came, but in a ring it can go A to B to C and back to A through a different interface, which split horizon allows.

options.text: Only when hold-down timers are also enabled
options.explanation: Hold-down is a mitigation, not a cause.

questions.workedExample: Consider a ring A–B–C with the only route to N originally through C. C loses N; A learns the failure but B still has stale reachability via C. B can advertise that stale route to A (a different interface from C). A can then advertise its newly selected route via B to C. C can select A, forming a three-router loop under suitable update ordering. Split horizon alone cannot detect the whole path. Additional controls and eventual unreachable information are required; link-state designs can also have transient forwarding loops during convergence.

lessons.title: Build an OSPF link-state database
lessons.summary: Trace OSPF neighbour discovery, adjacency selection, scoped OSPF LSA flooding and route computation.
lessons.body:
Trace OSPF neighbour discovery, adjacency selection, scoped OSPF LSA flooding and route computation.

## Link state and OSPF

### The idea

Instead of sharing distances, every router shares the raw facts about its own links. Everyone collects everyone's facts into the same map, then independently runs **Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm** on it. After the relevant databases and computations converge, routers can agree on valid shortest-path forwarding. During updates, transient disagreement and forwarding microloops remain possible.

**Open Shortest Path First** includes OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) for IPv4 and OSPFv3, originally for IPv6. OSPFv3 address-family extensions also support IPv4 (RFC 5838).

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A shared road atlas
> Instead of trusting signposts, every council publishes a sheet describing only its own roads and their lengths, and copies of every sheet are delivered to every council in the county. Each council binds the sheets into the same atlas and plans its own best routes from it.
>
> **How it maps:** A council's sheet is a router's link-state advertisement, the delivery of copies is flooding, the bound atlas is the link-state database, and route planning is each router running Dijkstra with itself as the starting point.
>
> **Where it stops:** Councils can plan from a slightly out-of-date atlas for a while; routers can too, which is why brief forwarding loops can occur while new LSAs spread. And OSPF limits each atlas to an area, so routers do not see the internal roads of every other area.

### How OSPF builds its map

1. **OSPF Hellos.** On enabled non-passive broadcast OSPFv2 interfaces, routers send Hello packets to 224.0.0.5. A common Cisco Ethernet configuration uses a 10-second Hello interval; other network types and configurations differ. Routers that hear each other and agree on parameters (area, timers, subnet) become **OSPF neighbours**. If no Hello arrives for the dead interval (40 seconds in that Cisco Ethernet configuration), the neighbour is declared down.
2. **Database sync.** Neighbours selected for adjacency exchange database description (DBD) packets and request missing LSAs. On a broadcast LAN, two DROther neighbours normally remain in the Two-Way state rather than forming a full adjacency; each instead synchronises its database with the DR and BDR.
3. **OSPF LSA flooding.** Router/network **link-state advertisements** (LSAs) describe area topology and are propagated within that area. LSA types have different scopes. Sequence numbers, checksums and age distinguish instances; standard self-originated LSAs are refreshed every LSRefreshTime, 1,800 seconds (30 minutes), even without a topology change, subject to protocol extensions.
4. **SPF.** Each router computes paths from its area **link-state database** (LSDB), using Dijkstra with itself as the root of the area topology. Inter-area and external routes require additional selection steps.

A detected failure causes affected originators to update LSAs. Depending on topology, DR role and changed reachability, more than the two link endpoints can originate updates. SPF scheduling, OSPF LSA flooding and forwarding installation determine how quickly routing convergence completes. Tuned designs can recover quickly, but no sub-second bound applies universally.

OSPF runs directly over IP (protocol 89), not over TCP or UDP, and handles its own reliability with acknowledgements.

## Pitfalls

- **Mismatched Hello or dead timers, MTU or area IDs**: OSPF neighbours get stuck short of full adjacency.
- **Inconsistent reference bandwidth** across routers gives asymmetric, surprising paths.
- **Flapping links** cause repeated SPF runs; implementations throttle SPF and LSA generation to stay stable.
- **Redistribution loops** between two protocols (OSPF into RIP and back) can create routing loops that neither protocol can see.

## Key takeaways
- OSPF routers build scoped link-state maps and compute paths after convergence.
- Not every pair of broadcast neighbours forms a full adjacency.
- Hello/dead intervals, area checks and database-exchange checks affect adjacency.
- Convergence includes detection, OSPF LSA flooding, computation and forwarding installation; no universal timing bound follows.

questions.prompt: In which kind of routing protocol does every router hold a map of the whole topology (within its area) and compute paths itself? Assume databases have converged.

options.text: Distance vector, like RIP
options.explanation: Distance-vector routers only know what their neighbours report: a distance and a next hop per destination. They never see the topology.

options.text: Link state, like OSPF
options.explanation: Correct. Each router floods LSAs describing its own links, every router collects them into an identical database, and each runs Dijkstra on that map.

options.text: Static routing
options.explanation: Static routes are typed in by people. No protocol builds a map.

options.text: Both; RIP and OSPF exchange the same information, only the timers differ
options.explanation: They exchange fundamentally different things: RIP sends distance tables, OSPF floods raw link-state facts.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask what each router sends.
2. RIP: "I can reach N in 3 hops" to neighbours only. A router's view is a list of rumours.
3. OSPF: "I am R5; I have a link to R2 cost 10 and to R7 cost 1" propagated to everyone in the area.
4. Only the second gives every router the full graph, so **link state** is the answer.

questions.prompt: Two OSPFv2 routers are intended to become fully adjacent on a broadcast Ethernet LAN (at least one is DR or BDR). Which differences can prevent that with ordinary checks enabled? Select all that apply.

options.text: Different Hello or dead intervals
options.explanation: Correct. Hello packets carry these timers and neighbours must agree, or they ignore each other's Hellos.

options.text: Different area IDs on the link
options.explanation: Correct. Both ends of a link must be in the same area.

options.text: Different interface MTUs
options.explanation: Correct. A database-description packet advertising an MTU larger than the receiver accepts is rejected, commonly preventing database exchange. Configured MTU-ignore behaviour can change this.

options.text: Different OSPF costs on each end
options.explanation: Cost is per interface and per direction. Different costs can affect path choices but do not inherently prevent adjacency or force asymmetric paths.

options.text: Different router priorities
options.explanation: Priority only affects DR/BDR election and is expected to differ between routers.

questions.workedExample: Hello/dead interval and area compatibility are checked in neighbour establishment. MTU is checked during database-description exchange unless overridden. Costs and priorities may differ without inherently blocking adjacency. The INIT state means bidirectional Hello visibility has not been established; it is not a unique diagnostic for a timer mismatch. On a broadcast LAN two DROther routers normally stay in the Two-Way state, so the question specifies that a full adjacency should exist.

lessons.title: OSPF interface costs and reference bandwidth
lessons.summary: Predict OSPF path choices under a reference-bandwidth cost model and spot when the default makes fast links look equal.
lessons.body:
OSPF picks the path whose interface costs add up to the smallest sum, so whatever sets the costs effectively sets the paths. A common default quietly makes all modern links look the same.

### Cost

Each interface has an **OSPF cost**, and a path's cost is the sum along it. Some implementations derive the interface cost from configured bandwidth: faster links get lower costs, until they hit a floor of 1.

```formula reference
C = max(1, ⌊R / B⌋)
where
C: the OSPF cost of the interface: a whole number with no unit; lower means more attractive
R: the reference bandwidth, in megabits per second (Mbit/s); 100 Mbit/s by default in classic Cisco IOS
B: the interface's configured bandwidth, in Mbit/s (1 Gbit/s = 1,000 Mbit/s)
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number, since costs are integers
max(1, …): the larger of 1 and the value after it, so the cost never falls below 1
Mbit/s: megabits per second: millions of bits per second
In words: the cost is the reference bandwidth divided by the link's bandwidth, rounded down, but never below 1. Any link at least as fast as the reference therefore gets the minimum cost of 1.
```

Classic Cisco IOS documentation uses a **100 Mbit/s** default reference, with a minimum positive interface cost of 1. Other platforms have different defaults, and cost can be manually configured; OSPF itself does not mandate this bandwidth formula. So:

| Link | Cost (ref 100M) | Cost (ref 100G) |
|---|---|---|
| 10 Mbit/s | 10 | 10,000 |
| 100 Mbit/s | 1 | 1,000 |
| 1 Gbit/s | 1 | 100 |
| 10 Gbit/s | 1 | 10 |

> [!warning] The 100 Mbit/s trap
> With the default, a 100 Mbit/s link and a 10 Gbit/s link both cost 1, so those interfaces have equal cost; hop structure and other costs then determine the path. Set the reference bandwidth higher (say 100 Gbit/s) on **every** router, consistently, or costs won't mean what you think.

## Key takeaways
- OSPF uses configured additive interface costs; the bandwidth formula is an implementation choice.
- The described 100 Mbit/s reference gives every faster interface the minimum cost of one.
- A higher consistent reference distinguishes modern links.
- Compare total path cost, not raw bandwidth or hop count alone.

## Further reading
- [RFC 2328: OSPF Version 2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2328)
- [RFC 2453: RIP Version 2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2453)

questions.prompt: An OSPF network uses a 100 Mbit/s reference bandwidth with minimum cost 1 and no manual cost overrides. An engineer upgrades a core link from 1 Gbit/s to 10 Gbit/s, expecting OSPF to move more traffic onto it, but the chosen paths do not change at all. Why?

options.text: OSPF ignores link speed entirely and counts only hops
options.explanation: OSPF uses configured interface costs, which in this setup are derived from bandwidth. The problem is how that derivation behaves above the reference.

options.text: The upgrade needs a full SPF recalculation, which OSPF only runs once a day
options.explanation: A cost change triggers new LSAs and SPF runs; there is no daily schedule. Here the cost simply did not change.

options.text: With a 100 Mbit/s reference, every link of 100 Mbit/s or faster already has the minimum cost of 1, so the link's cost is 1 before and after the upgrade
options.explanation: Correct. 100 divided by 1,000 or by 10,000 rounds down to 0, which is raised to the floor of 1. Raising the reference (consistently on every router) or setting costs manually lets OSPF tell these links apart.

options.text: Costs are only read when the routers reboot
options.explanation: Interface cost changes are advertised in new LSAs without a reboot. The cost here is unchanged.

questions.workedExample:
1. Under this model the cost is the reference bandwidth divided by the link bandwidth, rounded down, with a minimum of 1.
2. 1 Gbit/s: 100 / 1,000 = 0.1, raised to 1. 10 Gbit/s: 100 / 10,000 = 0.01, also raised to 1.
3. The cost stays 1, so no LSA changes the path calculation.
4. With a 100 Gbit/s reference on every router, the costs would be 100 and 10, and OSPF would prefer the faster link where it lowers the total.
5. Change the reference consistently, or a mix of references makes costs meaningless.

questions.prompt: R1 and R2 are joined directly by a 100 Mbit/s link, and also via R3 over two 10 Gbit/s links. OSPF uses a 100 Mbit/s reference bandwidth with minimum cost 1 and no manual overrides. Which path does R1 use to R2, and what changes if every router's reference is set to 100 Gbit/s?

options.text: Via R3 now (cost 2 beats nothing); unchanged at 100 Gbit/s
options.explanation: The direct link has cost 1, which beats the cost-2 path via R3. The default makes the slow link look best.

options.text: The direct 100 Mbit/s link now (cost 1 vs 2); via R3 after the change (cost 20 vs 1,000)
options.explanation: Correct. With ref 100M, every link of 100 Mbit/s or faster costs 1, so the single hop wins. With ref 100G the costs reflect bandwidth: 1,000 direct vs 10 + 10 = 20 via R3.

options.text: Both paths with ECMP, before and after
options.explanation: ECMP needs equal costs. 1 vs 2 isn't equal, and 1,000 vs 20 certainly isn't.

options.text: The direct link in both cases, because OSPF prefers fewer hops
options.explanation: OSPF minimises total routing cost, not hops. With a sensible reference, two fast links beat one slow one.

questions.workedExample:
The stated rule: each interface's cost is the reference bandwidth divided by its bandwidth, rounded down, with a minimum of 1. Path cost is the sum.

**Reference 100 Mbit/s**
- Direct 100 Mbit/s link: cost 1.
- Via R3: each 10 Gbit/s link would be 0.01, raised to the minimum of 1, so 1 + 1 = 2.
- 1 < 2: the slow direct link wins.

**Reference 100 Gbit/s**
- Direct: 100,000 / 100 = 1,000.
- Via R3: 100,000 / 10,000 = 10 per link, so 20.
- 20 < 1,000: the path over the faster links wins.

Change the reference on **every** router, or costs are inconsistent.

lessons.title: Trace a shortest-path-first calculation
lessons.summary: Follow a Dijkstra trace and carry each shortest path’s first hop into a forwarding decision.
lessons.body:
Every OSPF router runs the same calculation on its copy of the area map: Dijkstra's shortest-path-first algorithm, with itself as the starting point. Tracing one small example shows why a directly connected neighbour is not always reached over the direct link.

### A worked SPF

```
 A --1-- B
 |       |
 5       2
 |       |
 C --1-- D
 |       |
 3       5
 |       |
 +-- E --+
```

Dijkstra from A. Repeatedly settle the closest unsettled node and relax its links:

| Settle | Dist | Updates |
|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | B at 1, C at 5 |
| B | 1 | D at 3 |
| D | 3 | C at 4 (was 5), E at 8 |
| C | 4 | E at 7 (was 8) |
| E | 7 | none |

Every shortest path from A to another vertex in this graph starts via B, even to C, which A is directly connected to. A–B–D–C costs 4, beating the direct link's 5. A forwarding entry needs next-hop/interface information rather than the full path; implementations also retain metrics and other routing metadata.

Two properties make this work. Dijkstra settles nodes in order of distance, so once a node is settled its distance is final; that relies on link costs never being negative, which OSPF guarantees. And the router only needs the **first hop** of each shortest path for forwarding: every router on the path runs the same calculation on the same map, so each makes a consistent next choice.

The work grows roughly with the size of the map. With a binary-heap priority queue, the usual bound is O((V + E) log V), where V is the number of routers and networks and E the number of links. Implementations also limit how often SPF runs (throttling) and can recalculate incrementally; no measured run time is claimed here.

## Key takeaways
- Settle the least-distance candidate and relax outgoing links.
- Settled distances are final because costs are never negative.
- Forwarding needs only each shortest path's first hop; consistent maps give consistent choices.
- The example is a graph calculation, not a complete OSPF implementation or performance benchmark.

## Further reading
- [RFC 2328: OSPF Version 2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2328)
- [Dijkstra's algorithm — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijkstra%27s_algorithm)
- [Link-state routing protocol — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Link-state_routing_protocol)

questions.prompt:
Using the lesson's topology, router E runs SPF.

```
 A --1-- B
 |       |
 5       2
 |       |
 C --1-- D
 |       |
 3       5
 |       |
 +-- E --+
```

What is E's distance to D, and which first hop does E use?

options.text: 5, via the direct link to D
options.explanation: The direct routing link costs 5, but E–C–D costs 3 + 1 = 4, which is cheaper. Being directly connected doesn't mean shortest.

options.text: 4, via C
options.explanation: Correct. E settles C at 3, then relaxes C–D: 3 + 1 = 4, beating the direct 5.

options.text: 6, via C then B
options.explanation: E–C–A–B–D or similar paths are longer. D is reached directly from C.

options.text: 3, via C
options.explanation: 3 is E's distance to C. Add the C–D link (1) to reach D.

questions.workedExample:
Dijkstra from E:

| Settle | Dist | Updates |
|---|---|---|
| E | 0 | C at 3, D at 5 |
| C | 3 | A at 8, D at 4 |
| D | 4 | B at 6 |
| B | 6 | A at 7 |
| A | 7 | none |

D is settled at **4**, reached via C, so E's first hop for D is **C**.

lessons.title: Scale OSPF with areas and a DR
lessons.summary: Separate area topology scope from inter-area information and explain how a DR keeps broadcast-LAN adjacencies manageable.
lessons.body:
Link-state routing gives every router a full map, which gets expensive as networks grow. OSPF has two scaling tools: areas, which limit how far the detailed map spreads, and designated routers, which limit how many routers on a shared LAN must synchronise with each other.

### Areas

Propagating every LSA to every router and rerunning SPF on every change does not scale forever. OSPF splits a network into separate **OSPF areas**:

- **Area 0** is the backbone area. Inter-area routing uses backbone connectivity, which may include configured virtual links through suitable transit areas.
- **Area border routers** (ABRs) sit between areas. Inside an area, routers see the full topology. Other areas are represented by inter-area prefix/cost information rather than their internal topology. A summary LSA need not aggregate several prefixes unless aggregation is configured.
- An internal topology change in area 3 changes that area's topology LSAs. Other areas can receive changed inter-area reachability/cost information; how much route computation is rerun depends on the implementation and affected LSA types.

```
 [area 1]--ABR--[ area 0 ]--ABR--[area 2]
                    |
                  ASBR -- external routes
```

An **ASBR** (autonomous system boundary router) injects routes from outside OSPF, for example a default route from the Internet edge.

### Designated routers

On a shared segment like an Ethernet LAN, full adjacency between every pair of routers would grow quickly with their number. Instead the routers elect a **designated router** (DR) and a backup (BDR). Assume broadcast OSPF network type, compatible settings, an elected DR and BDR, and completed database synchronisation. Each other router (a "DROther") forms full adjacencies with those two rather than with every other router; the DR and BDR are also adjacent to each other. Pairs of DROthers still exchange Hellos but deliberately stop at the **Two-Way state**, so seeing them listed as 2WAY rather than FULL is normal, not a fault. The DR describes the shared segment in a network LSA.

```formula reference
A_mesh = n(n − 1) / 2
A_DR = 2(n − 2) + 1
where
A_mesh: the number of full adjacencies if every pair of routers formed one
A_DR: the number of full adjacencies with a DR and BDR
n: the number of OSPF routers on the shared segment, at least 2, under the broadcast/DR/BDR assumptions above
In words: in a full mesh every router pairs with every other, so the count grows roughly with the square of the number of routers. With a DR and BDR, each other router forms just two adjacencies, plus one between DR and BDR, so the count grows only in proportion. Ten routers need 45 adjacencies as a mesh but 17 with a DR.
```

With 20 routers the gap widens to 37 adjacencies instead of 190.

The election uses interface priority, then highest router ID, and is **not pre-emptive**: a newly arriving router with a higher priority does not displace an existing DR. Priority 0 makes an interface ineligible; when a DR fails an existing BDR can take over, rather than simply electing the newest highest-priority arrival.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A meeting chair and deputy
> In a large meeting, nobody briefs every other attendee one by one. Everyone reports to the chair, with a deputy taking notes in case the chair leaves, and the chair circulates the combined minutes.
>
> **How it maps:** The chair is the DR and the deputy the BDR. Each attendee keeps a full working relationship (an adjacency) only with those two, while still recognising everyone else in the room (the Two-Way state). The minutes are the network LSA describing the shared segment. A senior latecomer does not take the chair mid-meeting, just as DR election is not pre-emptive.
>
> **Where it stops:** The DR does not relay data traffic for the others; it only coordinates the routing database. Routers still forward packets directly to whichever neighbour is the best next hop.

## RIP vs OSPF

| | RIP | OSPF |
|---|---|---|
| Type | Distance vector | Link state |
| Metric | Hop-based cost | Configured interface cost |
| Knows | Neighbours' tables | Whole area map |
| Convergence | Depends on updates, failures and timers | Depends on detection, OSPF LSA flooding, computation and installation |
| Scale | Maximum usable metric 15 | Area design and implementation constrain scale |
| Config | Interfaces, routes, timers and policy | Areas, costs, timers and policy |

Other protocols include link-state **IS-IS** and distance-vector **EIGRP** with DUAL loop-avoidance logic. BGP can also be used within a data-centre fabric; RFC 7938 describes one such design rather than a universal deployment rule.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> Protocol market-share rankings, universal router-count limits and measured convergence-time comparisons are absent because no applicable deployment survey or benchmark was established. The worked SPF graph is a mathematical example, not a router benchmark.

## Key takeaways
- Area topology LSAs stay in their OSPF LSA flooding scope; inter-area information can still change.
- ABRs connect areas and ASBRs inject external routes.
- A DR/BDR reduces full adjacencies on a compatible broadcast LAN.
- DR election is non-pre-emptive; protocol choice and convergence depend on the design.

questions.prompt: Six OSPFv2 routers share one Ethernet LAN segment (broadcast network type, compatible configuration). On R5, which is neither DR nor BDR, the neighbour table shows the DR and BDR as FULL, and the other three routers as 2WAY. A colleague wants to open a fault ticket for the three 2WAY neighbours. What do you tell them?

options.text: It is a fault: every pair of OSPF routers on a LAN must reach FULL
options.explanation: On a shared segment with a DR, full adjacency with every router is exactly what the DR design avoids.

options.text: It is normal: DROthers form full adjacencies only with the DR and BDR and stay at Two-Way with each other, which keeps adjacencies growing in proportion to the routers rather than with their square
options.explanation: Correct. R5 synchronises its database through the DR and BDR. The three 2WAY neighbours are other DROthers; bidirectional Hellos are working, and no database exchange is needed between them.

options.text: It means the Hello and dead timers are mismatched on those three routers
options.explanation: Mismatched timers stop routers becoming neighbours at all; they would not appear in the Two-Way state.

options.text: It means those three routers have priority 0 and cannot route
options.explanation: Priority only affects DR/BDR eligibility. A priority-0 router still forms adjacencies with the DR and BDR and routes normally.

questions.workedExample:
1. On a shared broadcast LAN segment the routers elect a DR and BDR.
2. Every other router forms a full adjacency only with those two; the DR and BDR are also adjacent to each other.
3. DROther-to-DROther pairs see each other's Hellos (Two-Way) and stop there by design.
4. For six routers that means 9 full adjacencies instead of the 15 a full mesh would need, and the saving grows quickly with more routers.
5. Signs worth investigating would instead include a DR or BDR adjacency that never reaches FULL, neighbours stuck in the INIT state or in EXSTART, or expected neighbours missing entirely.

questions.prompt: An internal link in OSPF area 3 changes, altering a router LSA for that area. In which area's topology database is that LSA propagated and used for the area shortest-path calculation?

options.text: Every router in the whole OSPF domain
options.explanation: Router LSAs are area-scoped; the changed area-3 topology is not directly propagated throughout the entire domain.

options.text: Area 3, including the area-3 database of its ABRs
options.explanation: Correct. Other areas may receive inter-area reachability/cost changes, but do not receive area 3's internal router LSA as their own topology.

options.text: Only the two routers at the ends of the link
options.explanation: The changed topology LSA is propagated throughout its area, not just to the link endpoints.

options.text: Only area 0 routers, because the backbone computes routes for all areas
options.explanation: There's no central computation in OSPF. Each router runs SPF on its own areas' databases.

questions.workedExample: The area-3 router LSA remains in area 3. Routers attached to area 3, including ABRs, use that area database to compute topology paths. Changed costs or reachability can affect inter-area advertisements and calculations elsewhere. Implementations may batch, throttle or incrementally calculate routes, so this does not require one full SPF execution for every individual flap or guarantee all impact remains inside the area. Configured aggregation can hide some changes, not every possible failure.

lessons.title: Autonomous systems and AS paths
lessons.summary: Identify an autonomous system and interpret the reachability and loop-checking role of AS_PATH.
lessons.body:
OSPF computes paths within a routing domain using configured costs; that does not make its routers inherently trustworthy. Internet inter-domain routing must also accommodate independent networks, many of them competitors, with different policies. They need to exchange reachability without revealing their insides or giving up control.

That protocol is the **Border Gateway Protocol**, BGP-4 (RFC 4271). It's often called the glue of the Internet, and it runs on trust to a degree that surprises people.

## Autonomous systems

An **autonomous system** (AS) is a network under one administrative policy: an ISP, a cloud provider, a university, a large company. Public ASNs are allocated through Internet number registries; private ASNs can be used in appropriate private routing contexts.

- ASN fields expanded from 16 to 32 bits (RFC 6793). Not every encodable value is assignable: 65535 and 4294967295, for example, are reserved.
- Private ASN ranges exist for internal use: 64512–65534 and 4200000000–4294967294.
- AS numbers in the examples below illustrate routing policy; they are not instructions to announce those routes publicly.

Why the expansion? A 16-bit field can encode only 65,536 values, too few for every network that needed one; 32 bits allow about 4.3 billion. The reserved values 65535 and 4294967295 are the largest number each field size can hold.

An AS can use an IGP such as OSPF or IS-IS internally, alongside internal BGP. eBGP exchanges routes between ASes; designs can also use eBGP inside one organisation.

## A path-vector protocol

BGP is a **path-vector** protocol. Like distance vector, routers tell neighbours what they can reach. But instead of a distance, an ordinary **AS_PATH** sequence records advertised AS traversal, with repeated entries possible for prepending. It is not cryptographic proof of the actual forwarding path. For example:

```
203.0.113.0/24
  AS_PATH: 3356 1299 65010
            ^         ^
         neighbour   origin
```

That list does two jobs:

- **Loop prevention**: normal AS-loop checking excludes a received route containing the local ASN. Explicit configuration exceptions exist; this mechanism does not eliminate every possible forwarding loop or policy oscillation.
- **Policy**: operators can filter or rank the advertised path, subject to the limits of trusting that advertisement.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A parcel's chain of handlers
> Imagine each courier company that handles a parcel writes its name on a handling slip before passing it on. If a company receives a parcel whose slip already shows its own name, it knows the parcel has gone round in a circle and refuses it. A shipper can also choose between offers by how many handlers each would involve.
>
> **How it maps:** Each company is an AS, the slip is the AS_PATH, refusing a parcel with your own name on it is AS-loop checking, and choosing by number of handlers is the shortest-AS_PATH preference.
>
> **Where it stops:** Nothing stops a company writing a misleading slip: an AS_PATH is an unsigned claim, and networks can deliberately repeat their own name (prepending) to look longer. The slip describes the route announcement, not proof of where packets actually travel.

## Key takeaways
- ASNs have encoded values, private ASN ranges and other reserved values.
- An AS_PATH is an advertisement, not cryptographic proof of the forwarding path.
- Normal AS-loop checking excludes routes containing the local ASN.
- BGP exchanges policy-controlled reachability between independent networks.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4271: A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4271)
- [Border Gateway Protocol — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Gateway_Protocol)

questions.prompt: A BGP router in AS 65010 receives an eBGP update for 198.51.100.0/24 with AS_PATH `3356 65010 1299`. What does it do? Assume normal AS-loop checking with no configured exception.

options.text: Rejects the route, because its own ASN is already in the path
options.explanation: Correct. Normal AS-loop checking excludes this route because 65010 appears in its advertised path. The path is not proof of actual traffic traversal.

options.text: Accepts it and prepends 65010 again
options.explanation: Prepending happens when a router *sends* to an eBGP neighbour, and accepting a looped path is exactly what AS_PATH checking prevents.

options.text: Accepts it as the best route because the path is short
options.explanation: Path length only matters among acceptable routes. A path containing your own ASN is discarded before selection.

options.text: Forwards it to its iBGP peers to decide
options.explanation: Loop detection happens on receipt. The route is dropped, not passed around.

questions.workedExample:
1. The advertised sequence contains 3356, 65010 and 1299.
2. The receiver uses local ASN 65010.
3. With normal loop checking, the route is excluded because the local ASN occurs in that sequence.
4. This is an AS-loop check, not cryptographic verification of the path or a guarantee against every forwarding loop.

lessons.title: BGP sessions and route reflectors
lessons.summary: Trace BGP’s TCP session and compare base iBGP mesh requirements with reflection.
lessons.body:
BGP routers do not discover each other; operators configure each session. This lesson covers how a session stays alive, and why distributing routes inside one AS needs either a full mesh of sessions or route reflectors.

### Sessions

BGP routers ("speakers") form sessions over **TCP port 179**, using configured peer relationships. Base BGP has no OSPF-style multicast Hello discovery, although implementations can automate provisioning or accept dynamic peers under configured rules. Its four base message types are:

| Message | Purpose |
|---|---|
| OPEN | Start session, exchange ASN and proposed BGP hold time |
| UPDATE | Announce or withdraw prefixes |
| KEEPALIVE | Maintain liveness at a suggested interval of at most a third of the hold time |
| NOTIFICATION | Error; close the session |

Once established, the hold timer limits how long a router waits without an accepted KEEPALIVE or UPDATE before closing the session. RFC 4271 suggests a default hold time of 90 seconds and a KEEPALIVE interval of at most one third of the hold time (so 30 seconds for 90), giving the peer several chances to hear from it before the timer expires. BGP runs over TCP, so loss and retransmission delay when a complete message actually arrives.

After the initial permitted route exchange, normal updates are incremental. Route-refresh extensions can request re-advertisements. KEEPALIVE or UPDATE receipt can reset the hold timer; negotiated hold time zero disables this timer and KEEPALIVEs. Memory needs depend on prefixes, paths, attributes and implementation.

### eBGP and iBGP

- **eBGP** runs between different ASes, usually over a direct link.
- **iBGP** runs between routers in the *same* AS, to distribute BGP reachability internally, subject to selection and export policy.

iBGP does not prepend the local ASN, so the AS_PATH cannot record internal router traversal. In base iBGP, an iBGP-learned route is not re-advertised to another internal peer, so every BGP router must have a session with every other one, a full mesh:

```formula reference
S = n(n − 1) / 2
where
S: the number of iBGP sessions in a full mesh
n: the number of BGP routers in the AS
In words: every router needs a session with every other, so the number of sessions grows roughly with the square of the number of routers. 100 routers need 4,950 sessions, and adding one more router means configuring a new session on every existing router.
```

The reason for the full mesh is the rule itself: if R1 learns a route over eBGP and tells R2 over iBGP, R2 will not pass it on to R3. Unless R1 also has a session with R3, R3 never hears the route.

**Route reflectors** (RFC 4456) relax that restriction: selected client routes can be reflected to clients and non-clients, while non-client routes are reflected to clients. ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST support reflection-loop detection. With reflectors, each client needs sessions only to its reflectors. RFC 4456 notes that a cluster with a single reflector is a single point of failure, so clients usually peer with at least two. Confederations are another scaling approach.

## Key takeaways
- Base BGP uses configured TCP peer sessions on port 179.
- OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE and NOTIFICATION serve different purposes.
- A negotiated hold time of zero disables the hold timer and KEEPALIVEs.
- Route reflectors relax base iBGP redistribution restrictions and add loop-detection attributes.

questions.prompt: How do two BGP routers exchange routes?

options.text: Multicast Hellos discover neighbours automatically, like OSPF
options.explanation: Base BGP has no OSPF-style multicast Hello discovery. Peer relationships are configured, although implementations can automate provisioning or accept dynamic peers under rules.

options.text: Over UDP port 520 with periodic full-table updates
options.explanation: UDP port 520 and periodic routing updates describe RIPv2, not BGP.

options.text: Over a configured TCP session on port 179, sending incremental UPDATEs after the initial exchange
options.explanation: Correct. BGP uses TCP and normally incremental UPDATEs. KEEPALIVE and UPDATE messages maintain hold-timer liveness; extensions can request route refreshes.

options.text: Directly over IP as protocol 89
options.explanation: Protocol 89 is OSPF. BGP relies on TCP for reliability.

questions.workedExample:
1. Peer configuration establishes addresses, ASNs and policy.
2. A TCP session is opened to port 179.
3. OPEN exchanges session parameters and negotiated capabilities.
4. Initial advertisements contain the routes permitted by selection and export policy; subsequent updates normally describe changes.
5. For a nonzero negotiated hold time, KEEPALIVE or UPDATE receipt resets the timer. Expiry closes the session. Graceful-restart mechanisms can retain stale routes under specified conditions; a negotiated hold time of zero disables the hold timer.

questions.prompt: In AS 65010, border router R1 learns 198.51.100.0/24 from an eBGP neighbour. R1 has an iBGP session with R2, and R2 has an iBGP session with R3, but there is no R1–R3 session and no route reflection. R2 has the route; R3 does not. Why, and what are the standard fixes?

options.text: R3's IGP has not converged yet; wait a few minutes
options.explanation: IGP convergence does not decide whether an iBGP route is advertised. R2 is following a BGP rule and will never send this route to R3 as configured.

options.text: Base iBGP does not re-advertise routes learned from one internal peer to another, so R3 needs a session with R1 (full mesh), or R2 must be configured as a route reflector with R3 as a client
options.explanation: Correct. The rule exists because iBGP adds no AS to the path, so it cannot detect internal loops. A full mesh or route reflection (with ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST for loop detection) restores distribution.

options.text: R2 must prepend AS 65010 before sending to R3
options.explanation: iBGP does not prepend the local ASN, and prepending would not override the internal re-advertisement rule.

options.text: eBGP routes can never be shared inside an AS
options.explanation: Distributing externally learned routes inside the AS is exactly what iBGP is for; the issue is the missing session or reflector.

questions.workedExample:
1. R1 learns the route over eBGP and sends it to its iBGP peer R2.
2. RFC 4271: a speaker receiving an UPDATE from an internal peer shall not redistribute it to other internal peers, unless it is a route reflector.
3. So R2 keeps the route but does not tell R3.
4. Fix A: add an R1–R3 session. Taken to every router, this is the full mesh, whose session count grows roughly with the square of the number of routers.
5. Fix B: make R2 a route reflector with R3 (and R1 as needed) as clients, so each client needs sessions only to its reflectors.

lessons.title: Choose a BGP path by policy
lessons.summary: Predict which BGP route wins using local preference and a common selection order, while recognising vendor-specific rules.
lessons.body:
When a router hears several routes to the same prefix, BGP does not simply pick the shortest. It walks an ordered list of tie-breakers, and the first difference decides.

## Path attributes and best-path selection

Each route carries **path attributes**:

- **AS_PATH**: the advertised AS traversal, possibly including prepending.
- **NEXT_HOP**: where to send the traffic.
- **LOCAL_PREF**: a preference set *inside* your AS and shared over iBGP. Higher wins.
- **MED** (multi-exit discriminator): a hint from a neighbour about which of several links into it you should use. Lower wins.
- **BGP communities**: tags like `65010:100` that carry meaning by agreement, such as "don't announce this to peers" or "prepend twice towards Europe".

Among eligible routes for the same prefix, a common Cisco-style sequence is below. Reachability checks, vendor-specific steps (including Cisco weight before LOCAL_PREF), configuration and multipath settings matter; this is not a universal BGP ordering:

1. Highest **LOCAL_PREF**.
2. Prefer routes originated locally.
3. Shortest **AS_PATH**.
4. Lowest **origin attribute** (IGP, then EGP, then incomplete). These are attribute codes, not proof that the route was learned through an IGP.
5. Lowest **MED** (normally only between routes from the same neighbouring AS).
6. **eBGP** over iBGP.
7. Lowest IGP cost to the NEXT_HOP ("hot potato").
8. Further implementation-dependent tie-breakers, including route age in some eBGP cases and router IDs.

The key habit is to walk the list in order and stop at the first step where the routes differ. A later step, however lopsided, is never consulted.

> [!example] A worked choice
> Your AS hears 203.0.113.0/24 three ways:
> - From a transit provider: LOCAL_PREF 100, path `64500 3356 65010` (3 ASes).
> - From a peer: LOCAL_PREF 200, path `64600 64700 65010` (3 ASes).
> - From customer 65010 directly: LOCAL_PREF 300, path `65010 65010 65010` (prepended to 3).
>
> With all eligibility checks passed and earlier vendor-specific preferences equal, LOCAL_PREF decides: the customer route wins at 300. The customer's prepending was meant to push traffic away, but it only affects step 3, which is never reached.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Preferred suppliers
> A buyer's company policy says "use our preferred suppliers first; only if two are equally preferred, pick the one with fewer middlemen". A supplier who pads its quote with extra middlemen to discourage orders is still chosen if it is the preferred one.
>
> **How it maps:** The preferred-supplier ranking is LOCAL_PREF, set inside your own AS; the number of middlemen is AS_PATH length; padding the quote is AS_PATH prepending. Because policy is checked first, the padding only matters between equally preferred options.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real buyers might also weigh price or delivery time on the spot. Base BGP does not measure performance at all, and each router applies a fixed, vendor-defined order rather than judgement.

Note what's missing: bandwidth, latency, congestion. BGP picks paths by **policy** and AS count, not performance. The shortest AS_PATH may cross an ocean twice.

## Key takeaways
- Higher LOCAL_PREF can decide before AS_PATH length.
- Origin and MED have specific meanings and comparison conditions.
- Walk the selection order and stop at the first difference; later steps never override earlier ones.
- BGP path policy does not optimise measured latency, bandwidth or congestion.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4271: A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4271)
- [Cisco: BGP best-path algorithm](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/ip/border-gateway-protocol-bgp/13753-25.html)

questions.prompt: An ISP wants all outbound traffic to a prefix to leave via its cheap peering link rather than its expensive transit link, even though the transit path has a shorter AS_PATH. Which attribute should it set on routes from the peer? Assume both routes are eligible, visible to the relevant routers, and earlier vendor-specific preferences are equal.

options.text: A lower MED
options.explanation: MED usually influences entry into the advertising neighbour and is normally compared only for the same neighbouring AS. Under the stated ordering it follows AS_PATH.

options.text: A higher LOCAL_PREF
options.explanation: Correct. LOCAL_PREF is carried over iBGP and, with the earlier checks tied here, takes priority over AS_PATH length.

options.text: A longer AS_PATH via prepending
options.explanation: Prepending affects how *others* pick paths towards you, i.e. inbound traffic. And making the peer path longer would push traffic away from it.

options.text: A different NEXT_HOP
options.explanation: NEXT_HOP identifies a forwarding next hop. Changing it can affect eligibility or later IGP-cost tie-breaks, but is not the stated direct way to rank the peer route ahead of transit before AS_PATH.

questions.workedExample:
1. The decision concerns outbound routing within the AS.
2. Both eligible routes pass earlier checks equally.
3. Assign LOCAL_PREF 200 to the peer route and 100 to transit.
4. LOCAL_PREF decides before path length.
5. Consistent policy and visibility of the preferred route are needed across the AS; iBGP does not guarantee identical information at every router.

questions.prompt:
A router has two eBGP routes for the same prefix, both with origin IGP:

| | LOCAL_PREF | AS_PATH | MED |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | 100 | 64500 64501 65010 | 10 |
| Y | 100 | 64600 65010 | 50 |

Which is chosen? Assume both are eligible and equally weighted, with no local origination or configuration overriding the lesson’s selection order.

options.text: X, because its MED is lower
options.explanation: MED is checked only after AS_PATH length. And X and Y come from different neighbouring ASes, so their MEDs wouldn't normally be compared at all.

options.text: Both, load-balanced, since LOCAL_PREF ties
options.explanation: A LOCAL_PREF tie just moves on to the next step. BGP multipath requires a tie through many more attributes.

options.text: X, because it was received first
options.explanation: Route age can be a late eBGP tie-breaker on some implementations; it cannot overcome the AS_PATH difference under the stated order.

options.text: Y, because its AS_PATH is shorter (2 vs 3)
options.explanation: Correct. LOCAL_PREF ties at 100, there's no local origination, so AS_PATH length decides: 2 ASes beats 3.

questions.workedExample:
Walk the order:

1. LOCAL_PREF: 100 vs 100, tie.
2. Locally originated: neither.
3. AS_PATH length: X has 3 ASes, Y has 2. **Y wins.**

Selection stops here. MED (step 5) never comes into it, and would normally be skipped anyway because the routes come from different neighbours (64500 vs 64600).

lessons.title: Commercial routing and traffic engineering
lessons.summary: Trace simplified customer, peer and provider export policy and explain traffic-steering limits.
lessons.body:
Trace simplified customer, peer and provider export policy and explain traffic-steering limits.

## The economics: who carries whose traffic

Relationships between ASes are commercial:

- **Customer to provider**: the customer pays for transit to the whole Internet.
- **Inter-AS peering**: two networks exchange agreed traffic; settlement-free peering has no traffic settlement payment between them, but paid peering and infrastructure costs also exist.

A simplified commercial policy consistent with the **Gao–Rexford** model is shown below. Preferring customers over peers/providers is the key ranking restriction here; ranking peers above providers is an additional illustrative choice, not required by their Guideline A:

| Learnt from | Prefer | Export to |
|---|---|---|
| Customer | Most (they pay you) | Everyone |
| Peer | Middle | Customers only |
| Provider | Least (you pay) | Customers only |

The export rule produces **valley-free** paths: traffic goes up through providers, across at most one peer link, and down through customers. Under these BGP export restrictions a network does not provide transit between its providers. Real contracts and routing policies can differ; results about BGP convergence require additional model assumptions, including an acyclic customer-provider hierarchy.

### Traffic engineering

Operators steer traffic with the tools above:

- **LOCAL_PREF** controls which way traffic *leaves* your network.
- **AS_PATH prepending** (adding your own ASN several times) makes a path look longer, to discourage traffic *entering* via that link. Neighbours' LOCAL_PREF overrides it.
- **More-specific prefixes**: announce a /23 everywhere and two /24s from different sites. Where those more-specific routes are accepted and installed, longest-prefix match selects them.
- **Anycast**: announce the same prefix from many locations. Routing policy selects one reachable announcement; this need not be the geographically closest or lowest-latency site. DNS services can use this arrangement.

RFC 7454 documented IPv4 **/24** and IPv6 **/48** as common public-routing specificity limits in 2015, while explicitly allowing those practices to change. Acceptance depends on the receiving network and its current policy. More-specific routes can be useful in private or explicitly agreed routing; no announcement length guarantees that a route spreads everywhere.

## Key takeaways
- The Gao–Rexford model imposes ranking/export constraints and additional hierarchy assumptions.
- LOCAL_PREF steers outbound choice; prepending only influences neighbours that reach that comparison.
- Accepted more-specific routes steer their covered destinations.
- Anycast routing need not select the geographically closest or fastest site.
